Second report of standing committee on agriculture and colonization.-Mr. Weir.

Labour Conditions

subtopic: INQUIRY WITH RESPECT TO DELEGATION ON FARM LABOUR SITUATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY WITH RESPECT TO DELEGATION ON FARM LABOUR SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Labour, who I think is the appropriate minister, although three ministers are involved. I understand that a delegation of farmers met three ministers, as well as the director of national selective service, in Ottawa yesterday and presented a resolution endorsed by thirty-six Ontario county units of the federation of agriculture, which resolution contained constructive proposals for relieving the present acute farm labour situation. Will the Minister of Labour indicate to the house the nature of these proposals, as well as the steps which the government is prepared to take with respect to them?

subtopic: INQUIRY WITH RESPECT TO DELEGATION ON FARM LABOUR SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not the
resolution with me, as this matter came on my desk just before I entered the house. We did have a conference with the delegation, and I would say a very successful conference. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has intimated, the delegation met two other ministers as well as myself, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). As my hon. friend is well aware, we have an agreement with every province in Canada respecting the placement of farm labour, not only in the summer months but the whole year round, and these agreements have worked very satisfactorily in every province. But in addition, after hearing the representations of the delegation it was decided that a committee, accompanied by an official of the Department of Labour, would meet the district officers commanding at Toronto, London, Kingston, Petawawa and Borden with a view to speeding up the granting of leave to men who wish to go farming to the fullest possible extent consistent with army needs.
We also telegraphed the ministers of agricv.I ture for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba with a view to moving an additional 500 experienced farmers from the western prairies to eastern Canada so that they would be able to help harvest the heavy crops in eastern Canada. We had a similar movement last year. The hon. gentleman will understand that the crops this year in the east are heavier than last year.	[DOT]
It has also been decided to recruit 500 students, seventeen years of age or over, who have had farming experience or who come from farm homes in western Canada to give us some assistance with the very heavy crop in this part of the country.
A letter has also gone out to all the industrialists of Ontario urging upon them the desirability of releasing as many experienced farm workers as possible, consistent with maintaining war production, to assist in harvesting the crop.
In addition to that, I might say that we are of course working in very close cooperation with the Department of Agriculture of Ontario, as we did last year. Last year we placed over 100,000 on the farms of Ontario through the instrumentality of that cooperation. I have also sent a direct appeal to the mayors and other municipal officials of all the municipalities in Ontario in an effort to ensure wherever possible the granting of leave to municipal employees in order that we may get over the hump of the haying season and the peak of the farm season in Ontario.

maintopic: STRIKE AT UNITED SHIPYARDS LIMITED, MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I would like to ask the Minister of Labour:
1.	Has a strike occurred in the plant of United Shipyards, Limited, at Montreal?
2.	If so, what steps are being taken by the federal Department of Labour to settle the dispute?
3.	Has the union holding the collective bargaining agreement asked for police protection because of the attitude of a minority of the workers?

maintopic: STRIKE AT UNITED SHIPYARDS LIMITED, MONTREAL
speechtext:
I will answer the first and last questions first. A strike has taken place in the United Shipyards in the city of Montreal, engineered by a minority group there. The union in question has asked for protection in order to permit the membership to go to work in an orderly manner. Arrangements have been made that every protection will be given to those union workers in that particular shipyard to see to it that they carry out the terms of their agreement so that the construction of these very necessary ships at this critical time in the nation's history will be proceeded with.

Aeronautics Act
On the orders of the day:

I wish to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. I regret that I have not sent him notice of the question but it is of such a nature that perhaps notice is not required. On June 29 I asked a question with regard to the situation which was alleged in military district No. 1 at London, Ontario. Has any investigation been made since that time and has any irregularity been discovered? Because of the nature of the answer to my question on that day, I ask this supplementary question now. I understand that recently a further investigation has been made and it is alleged that some grave irregularities have been discovered.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: I wonder if my hon. friend would remind me of the question to which he refers.

The question I asked1, as reported at page 4334 of Hansard, was:
I.	Will the Minister of National Defence inform the house whether an investigation has been instituted into alleged irregularities at the central mechanization depot in London, Ontario? 2. If such an investigation has taken place, what irregularities, if any, have been discovered? 3. Has the attention of the minister been drawn to the possibility of irregularities in other divisions of military district No. 1, and will the minister consider instituting an investigation into the administration of the entire district?
I remember now. The investigation, I believe, is still proceeding. 1 have not had any report on it at all but I shall inquire.

CIVIL AVIATION AND COMMERCIAL AIR SERVICES-[DOT] AIR TRANSPORT BOARD
The house resumed from Wednesday, June 21, consideration in committee of bill No. 133, to amend the Aeronautics Act-Mr. Michaud -Mr. McCann in the chair.
On section 1-New heading inserted.

When this matter was last before the committee some reference was made to the fact that certain provinces might feel constrained to establish air companies within their confines because of the restrictive nature of the provisions of this bill from the standpoint of air development. The minister indicated that under the aeronautics case the jurisdiction of the federal government was supreme, and inferentially that the provinces could not establish any inter-

urban, intercity or intertown air services. Has the matter been submitted by the minister's department to the Department of Justice with a view to ascertaining whether the provinces have or have not that power? I have looked over the aeronautics case and it would indicate that, within the powers of the several provincial legislatures under section 92, air companies could be started by a province and operated by the province, subject only to the control of the dominion authority in so far as safety regulations, the qualifications of airmen, and so on.
As I read the privy council appeal from the aeronautics case reference 30 Supreme Court Reports, 663, it appears to me that flying within the province itself could be engaged in by provinces. The reason I mention that is that everywhere in the United States to-day there is widespread development to meet the post-war air situation, while little or nothing is being done in this country. On July 6, as reported at page 4551, I asked a question with regard to the purchase of land for airport purposes. I wanted to know whether any land had. been purchased in Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina, Winnipeg and Malton, and the only purchases that have been made were certain purchases at Edmonton, Vancouver and Regina. If when the war is over we are to assure our returning air men of an opportunity for work and an opportunity to serve, it cannot be done under the present provisions of the present bill. In the United States, in order to assure availability of jobs for as many returned men as possible, the C.A.A. is increasing its airports and believes that by the time the war is over some 6,000 will be established in the smaller cities or towns, provided the air service plans now being developed as a result of competition between private enterprises on interurban service are put into effect.
In 1941 there were only seventy-six airports with runways thirty-five hundred feet long or more; to-day there are eight hundred and sixty-five. In other words, because the air companies in the United States- have an opportunity to compete and to set up services between cities and larger urban centres the government of that country is making preparations to expand interurban and other facilities. In Canada the future of air development is uncertain. If the government is to take over the airways of this country it can never hope to meet the needs in the establishment of air fleet systems between cities and towns in what may be called bus line service. Take the city of Winnipeg as an example. That city is on the line for the development of a world service, and yet to-day it has not the air

Aeronautics Act
facilities that it must have in anticipation of post-war development. Saskatoon and Prince Albert in northern Saskatchewan are other examples. Prince Albert is the centre of development of air transportation into the north in Saskatchewan, yet there is no suggestion of airways or an airport to meet the potentialities of the post-war period.
If the provinces have the right to enter into interurban airways, my submission is the transportation facilities and needs within those provinces will be met much more readily and much sooner than if the matter remains entirely subject to the authority of the government airways. Only recently in the welcoming the incoming president of the institute of mining and metallurgy, Mr. Drew, speaking at Toronto, is reported in the press to have said:
Canada is far behind other countries in development o-f interurban air transport. Taking Ontario as an example, covering an area equal in size to a considerable part of Europe, only five communities are served by regular air transport. They are Toronto, London, Windsor, Ottawa and North Bay.
At a meeting of the aeronautical institute it passed resolutions asking that something be done to give small private enterprises the opportunity to apply now for licences to place smaller towns and cities of this country on the air maps by making provision for the development of air service between them. What consideration has been given to this matter? It would in no way interfere with the rights of the Trans-Canada Air Lines' across-Canada service. It would provide an incentive and an opportunity for small companies to build up air bus lines between cities and towns within the various provinces. It is being done in the United States, and according to the latest records so much interest is being taken in the.matter that applications by the thousands are being made to this end and are being decided now by the aeronautical authorities in charge of this administration.
When the board is set up the minister should give the assurance that in so far as interurban or intercity routes are concerned the board will consider applications now for the setting up of companies and the allocation of lines. I do not say that that could be done with all important routes, not by any means. But consideration should be given to a sufficient number so that development will be under way when the men in the air force come back from overseas, and they will find something available for them to do. If that is not done, when they are demobilized they will return to civilian life and will not be able to use the knowledge and technical skill which they have received during war service,
and the failure to provide opportunities for them will result in their gradually going into some other line of work in civil life.
I understand that there are applications from Ontario and Quebec before the present board asking for the right to operate private lines on short air routes that by no means could be operated by a central authority. What are the plans in regard to the development of airports? I mentioned only a few of them-Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon and Prince Albert. What is being done now? What are the plans for the immediate future? Has the government given consideration to having the air transport board appointed at once and given the right immediately to consider applications and make decisions? I do not wish to repeat my premise, but if that were done there would be available, in part at least, an opportunity for these returned airmen to be absorbed in an occupation for which they have been highly trained and for which they have every qualification.

The first point raised was as to whether or not the provinces have the right to control civil aeronautics operations within their own boundaries. My reading of the aeronautics decision indicated to me that they had not that right. The domain of the air comes under federal jurisdiction. However, I may say we have had no application from any province to exercise that right. I understand that we are about to receive one. Recently the premier of Ontario made a speaking tour in the north country, during which he promised provincial air transport services to a number of communities in that area. When that application is received, we shall be very glad to consider it. In the meantime we assume that Mr. Drew will be active in building the necessary facilities such as airports, radio ranges and all the aids to navigation that that enterprise involves. Therefore I think that that question can very well wait until Mr. Drew's application is received. I expect to remind him from time to time that he has made the promises, and I will continue to urge that he carry them out.
The next question had to do with the lack of expansion of air facilities. The hon. member mentioned the expansion of a number of aerodromes in the United States during war years. May I point out that the expansion of facilities in Canada is in proportion considerably greater than that of the United States. All aerodromes that have been built in the United States during the war period have been built for war purposes. In the same way
Aeronautics Act

every aerodrome in Canada that has been built during the war period has been built for war purposes.
Is that true in the United States?
Yes.

That is not my
reading of it.

Then tell me of one not built for war purposes. Surely my hon. friend must have some examples. He should not expect me to answer vague questions and then, without knowing the facts, challenge my answer.
The minister's denial has too often been the highest corroboration of the truth of the statement denied.
Well, when my hon. friend suggests that hundreds have been built he should be able to mention one.
Yes, I said there were hundreds.

But my hon. friend cannot mention one. The hon. gentleman implied that there had been a great expansion of civil aviation in the United States during the war years. As a matter of fact there are fewer civilian transport planes flying in the United States to-day than there were at the outbreak of war, just as there are fewer planes on our own purely civilian operations in Canada today than there were at the beginning of the war. Aviation authorities in the United States have taken the view that the facilities of the industry should be devoted wholly to war purposes, and Canada has taken the same view. We have built in this country an immense number of planes, I believe more than twelve thousand. All these planes have been military types with one exception, a transport type which has been used almost exclusively for war purposes.
My hon. friend suggests that there is activity in the United States now in connection with the hearing of applications for new routes. That is true; the hearings were opened a few months ago, and if this act is endorsed by parliament it is intended to follow a similar procedure in Canada. That is, applications for routes will be received and considered. That is the purpose in establishing the board provided for under the act now before parliament. Have I covered the ground? '
There was one question with which the minister* did not deal. Has there been any submission to the Department of Justice on the question-

This bill was drafted by the Department of Justice. I have not asked for an opinion, because I have had no reason to be interested in an opinion. If an application is received an opinion will be obtained. I may add that the jurisdiction of the United States over aviation within a state was challenged, and the fact was established that it is a matter coming under federal jurisdiction.
But their constitution is different from ours in respect to the allocation of residuary powers.

Perhaps. If anyone cares to challenge the ruling given by the privy council in the aeronautics case, we shall be glad to get an opinion from the Department of Justice. In the meantime it is purely an academic matter.

The minister has
stated that if anyone wants to challenge the decision of the government he will be given an opportunity to do so. Is that it?
No, I did not say that. I said if they want to challenge the ruling in the aeronautics case, which was taken to the privy council, and which stated that the air comes under federal jurisdiction-

That is exactly the point I wanted the minister, to clarify. Now I am going to ask the minister, when he comes to the section dealing with the board itself, to make provision for an appeal to the courts in any question of law or jurisdiction. As the situation now is-and the minister has given the best possible argument that could be advanced for it-when the war is over, or even before, the question will be raised by the province of Ontario as to the right of that province to operate interurban airways within its own boundaries. As the bill is now set up the decision would be made by the air transport board, with no* right of appeal to the courts to determine the legality of the decision
I would ask my hon. friend, as a lawyer, whether anyone cannot take a constitutional issue to the courts.

Oh, Mr. Chairman; a constitutional issue can go to the courts only when it is submitted as a reference, as it was in the aeronautics case, or as the result of litigation, and there can be no litigation if a transport board is set up by this parliament and given the absolute power to determine when, where and under what circumstances a licence shall be granted. Their decision is final. On several occasions when I have dealt with this matter I have endeavoured to make the

Aeronautics Act
point that parliament must not permit the setting up of a board above the courts, to which the subject may not have recourse. The minister says that if and when an application is received from Colonel Drew on behalf of the province of Ontario the matter will receive consideration, and that if anyone wishes to challenge the judgment in the aeronautics case an opportunity will be given to do so. Provision therefore is not contained in this act. That is why I say it is so necessary that the decisions of this board on matters of law and jurisdiction should be subject to an appeal to the courts by any aggrieved party. Otherwise the minister will be able to say to the province of Ontario when that application is made-for after all no licence can be issued by the board without the approval of the minister-"we refuse to give you a licence," and neither the province of Ontario nor any other province will have the opportunity of testing in the courts their right to operate an airway, because no one can operate a plane unless he possesses a federal licence. No one can act as pilot of a plane unless he has a federal licence. So all the minister would have to do would be to refuse a licence to the province, and there would be no recourse to the courts.
That is why I have been endeavouring on several occasions to make the point that under this act the government is setting up a board not responsible to the people of Canada; not responsible to the courts, however unjust its decisions may be, but responsible only to the minister. I object to placing such power in the hands of any minister.
I ask the minister to say why the right of recourse to the courts is taken away. Under the former transport board, which among other things had to do with air transportation, there was provision for an appeal to the courts. That specific provision was contained in section 52 of the Railway Act, which was made applicable to the Transport Act, in these words:
2.	An appeal shall lie from the board to the Supreme Court of Canada upon a question of jurisdiction, upon leave therefor being obtained from a judge of the said court. . . .
3.	An appeal shall also lie from the board to such court upon any question which in the opinion of the board is a question of law, or a question of jurisdiction, or both. . . .
These rights of appeal are taken away in connection with, the board now being set up. Similar rights exist in Great Britain and the United States, but here we are setting up a board controlled by one individual, the minister, and not providing any right of recourse to the courts. This becomes of particular importance at the present time, when there is
the suggestion that the premier of Ontario is going to endeavour to set up aviation facilities within this province.
That is a promise, not a suggestion.

Yes, it is a promise. And the minister says he is going to remind him of the promise. The minister is the man who will determine whether or not the promise can be carried into effect. Does that not show the true picture? All the minister has to do to-day, is to say that the opportunity will be given, if asked for, so that the promise can be carried into effect. All the minister has to do to-day is to allow an amendment to the transport regulations so that reference can be had to the courts if the application is denied. Only in that way, when the board acts unfairly in a matter of jurisdiction, would Ontario or any other province have the right of recourse to the courts. The minister says he will help the premier of Ontario; at the same time I ask him to make it possible for that promise to be carried into effect by making provision for an appeal which does not exist at the present time should the province's application be denied.
More opportunity for the legal fellows to get work.
I did not hear my hon. friend.
Just more opportunity for legal fellows to get more work.
Who?
Legal fellows-lawyers, like yourself. The hon. member does not understand me.
Well, that is a remark which certainly shows an intelligent view of what is being discussed!
Just as intelligent as your interpretation of the act.
The remark was far removed from what I was discussing.

Your attitude is quite
apparent.

I think every other member understands what I am endeavouring to say, because I have been outlining a principle of responsible government, and the right of the individual to an appeal from the decision of the boards. If this one is set up. it will go a long way farther than any other board ever set up by this parliament, and will not be responsible even to the governor in council. It is responsible only to the minister. Aeainst that I make my protest. And I am asking the minister whether he will consider
Aeronautics Act

giving an opportunity for an appeal, so all individuals, however great or however small they may be, will have equal opportunity and equal access to justice by making provision for appeal to the courts.

If I am asked to rule on legal questions I shall be glad to do so. The hon. member must know that the Aeronautics Act does not preclude the province from obtaining a legal decision as to its right to operate air lines within the province. I can tell him how they can get such a decision, without any trouble at all, namely, by operating an air line without obtaining a licence under this act.
The pilot cannot operate as he is subject to cancellation of his licence.

The pilot can operate without any trouble, depending upon his record. A licence can only be taken away for cause. However, this represents the logical way of doing things. That is the way it was done in New York state. An operation was set up there, and the matter was referred to the courts. The same procedure can follow here. I suggest that my hon. friend give legal' advice as to why it cannot be done that way.
That is what I have done.
As an engineer I dislike to give a legal opinion to a lawyer, although sometimes I find it is desirable to do so, just to keep the record straight.
You have fifteen lawyers in the cabinet. They should know.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Good ones, too.
That is about ten too many.

I may say this, that if the province or anybody else wishes to take the responsibility for establishing an air line, I hardly think any obstacles will be placed in their way. Each application will be judged on its merits. The intention is, as soon as this act passes, to set up a board-just as strong a board as it is possible to appoint, and to proceed vigorously to develop a postwar system of aviation for Canada.
My hon. friend does not say positively that all the services are to be government owned, but he keeps hinting at that. Such is not the case. That is not the intention. I have said many times that the Trans-Canada system is government-owned, and will continue to be government-owned. But it is the purpose to develop subsidiary operations as private operations under this act.

The minister referred to certain promises having been made by the premier of Ontario, while he was in the norths western part of the province. I take it that the minister himself, knowing the situation so far as air transportation up there is concerned, would be favourable to the kind of undertaking the premier of Ontario suggested should be carried out.
Perhaps my hon. friend can just tell me what kind of undertaking it is- something about it. He just said he was going to build air lines.
And on that score, perhaps the minister would indicate his approval or disapproval of the suggestion.

The federal government had built a fairly complete system of air services throughout the north country. There is a missing link, required to give service to Fort William and Port Arthur-my own riding: Perhaps if I had been as aggressive as some of riiy predecessors in office, the link would have been closed. However, I thought it was better to let those links develop naturally. There is a fine airport in the area, and it is the intention, as soon as we can get suitable equipment, to serve Port Arthur and Fort William with a direct air lane operating between Winnipeg and Toronto. That has been made abundantly clear. Premier Drew knew all that when he made his speech at Port Arthur. But that is rather beside the discussion here. When we compare the present system of air transportation in northern Ontario with that which served the area in 1935, when my hon. friend's party turned over the reins of office to this government, it will be seen that there has been a vast improvement.
I suppose that is because of a general development throughout the world. * I understand that.
There was a great development throughout the world until 1935, too.
I do not wish to take anything away from my hon. friend in the matter; nevertheless I think he will find that there has been a development in air transportation throughout the world generally.
In 1935 Canada led the world in air transport by freight.
How much in northern Ontario?
I knew what was going on at that time.

It is about northern
Ontario I wish to say a word now. I do not

Aeronautics Act
like to see this conflict between the minister and the premier of Ontario. I would like to feel that their interests are the same, and that both desire to develop northern Ontario.
I am convinced that the chambers of commerce which met at Fort Frances recently, and who were addressed by the Premier of Ontario, had the same object in mind, the development of that country. I have been asking myself just how the government of Ontario, or for that matter any government of any other province wishing to do the same thing, could develop its hinterland. However I shall confine my remarks to Ontario, and as to how the government of that province can develop the north country. I know the minister himself is very much in favour of such development.
I have tried to arrange for a plane trip to the Belcher islands, and to the Clark islands, up in Hudson bay, to examine the iron deposits there. I have not been able to get that service. The Ontario government might want to develop an air transport line to the Hudson bay coast, and it might also wish to develop air lines to bring back the iron resources to the mills at Sault Ste. Marie. I am sure that the plane industry will develop planes of 500 tons capacity. Just a few days ago we read of a plane carrying 50 tons of freight and something over 50 passengers from Africa to America. I think it is easy to envision 500 ton aeroplanes. If that comes to pass I can see a fleet of 500-ton transport planes carrying ore from Clark island and Belcher islands down to the smelter at Sault Ste. Marie. How can Ontario give encouragement to a private company to start up a transport line of this kind when they are limited by this bill? This ore is needed to operate the smelting plant at Sault Ste. Marie, and later there might be a great smelting plant in the minister's own city. The high grade ore will be brought down from Steep Rock, which is northwest of Fort William, and low grade ore will be required to mix with it. Belcher islands' ore would help.
I am alarmed, perhaps because I do not-know enough about it, over just how much this bill is going to prevent private development. I really know little about the legality of these items, but the hon. member for Lake Centre is a celebrated lawyer. I anf not one to make jokes about lawyers. I like to keep put of their hands as much as I can, and I like to keep out of the courts. But he does know what he is talking about and apparently he is much alarmed about this bill, which confines the air transport business to a board which is to be clothed with supreme powers but which also is under the control of the minister.
The hon. member suggested that there should be the right of appeal to the courts. What objection can there be to that? I cannot see any. Surely there should be an appeal from the minister to the courts on whether or not a licence should be granted, and I support the hon. member in that regard.
Coming back to where I started, I am very much concerned about whether this measure will encourage the development of northern Ontario, and I am confining myself to that part of the country. The whole north end of the province adjacent to Hudson bay, while not all tundra, does contain a great deal of muskeg. . The development of the area, from the plateau on which the Albany river flows, down to the bay cannot be carried on by the building of railroads. What better method of transporting ore could be developed than by air? I appreciate Colonel Drew's desire to develop northern Ontario and I do not think the minister should consider it as being politics. I do not say that he does. I am afraid that there will be objection to the construction of branch air lines in that north country and I am strongly in favour of the Ontario government or any other provincial government being able to construct their own lines.
My hon. friend (Mr. Diefenbaker) comes from Prince Albert-a beautiful and splendid city, a city with a great future. It should develop into one of our greatest airports, because it has everything in the way of topography and territory for the creation of an important air transport centre. It should be the centre of air transport into the country right through to lake Athabaska and east of lake Athabaska. That country is full of lakes and rivers, but it is also full of minerals. I can envision my hon. friend's city of Prince Albert becoming a great centre of aeroplane transport service. Would Saskatchewan be allowed to develop a line?
It has a service now, and has had for years.
It is not an air transport service.

Oh, yes, it is.
Mr. MaeJCICOL: Not 50- and 100-ton planes. There are a few running up the Alaska highway, but that is not in Saskatchewan.
There is no such thing as a 100-ton plane or a 50-ton plane.

I know a few planes run north from Prince Albert to Goldfields and Yellowknife, but those are mail planes although they carry a few passengers. I am thinking of the transport planes that carried in machinery
Aeronautics Act

to Yellowknife and to the north side of lake Athabaska. I am pretty sure they belonged to the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company. I know they had their own planes which took in a lot of freight.
We should all wish to see this country opened up, and an aeroplane service is one means of doing it. I do not like to oppose the minister's suggestion, because he has given it a lot of thought, but I am firmly convinced that this country could be opened up more rapidly and more profitably by having competitive services in air transport. I am not speaking now of Trans-Canada, although in that case I think after the war-the minister is a business man and he will appreciate this- air transport could be carried on better by the great rail transport companies.
I hold no brief for the Canadian Pacific or for the Canadian National. I want them both to succeed, but how can the Canadian Pacific develop a great transport business in the air? So far as I can see, it cannot do it under this bill; yet I think it should be able to do it. The Canadian Pacific has been one of the greatest agencies in the opening up of this country. Both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National have the necessary facilities in the great cities like Montreal. They have the trained personnel, and it seems to me to be unbusinesslike to prevent a great companylike the Canadian Pacific from participating in the air transport field. I am sure that after this war aeroplanes will not stop at 500 tons; there is no reason why they should not go up to 1,000 tons capacity.
The Canadian Pacific is the largest transport company-if not the largest it is the second largest-in Canada, and I do not think that company, or the Canadian National, should be prevented from opening up this country by means of air transport, and any others who want to start should not be prevented. I feel satisfied that we are heading in the wrong direction. I cannot add anything more to what I have said. I have expressed my opinion as to what I think about the ability, of private industry to open up the country. I have seen and heard1 enough about private industry to know this. I have heard private industry denounced in this house, but I know that many businesses have been kept going by men who have sat up all night trying to develop and advance their industry.
It would not be possible to have that in a government-operated organization. Men in government-operated plants do not sit up all night. I have been through it and I know. Time without number I have sat up all night week in and week out trying to develop and
fMr MacNicoI.]
advance big business. Money cannot pay for that; you must have the heart and will to develop. Men in a government-operated plant will not do it; they never have and I do not expect they ever will. I am not going to say anything against the Canadian National. It has been a fine company and has done a fine job. The same can be said about the T.C.A. Some one took out of something I said that I was not an advocate of the T.C.A. I have not said anything in opposition to the T.C.A. It has been well managed and has done splendid work and will continue to do so. But that does not detract in any way from the strength of my advocacy of private operation, private incentive and private enterprise.
I am supporting the hon. member for Lake Centre in his desire to have an appeal to the courts of the land. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Except for some of the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport it seems to me that a good deal of the discussion we have had thus far this afternoon has skirted the real issue which has been put before us by the introduction of this bill. We have had discussion about provincial rights and constitutional questions, and we have had cross-fire between the minister and a provincial premier who is not here. But the real issue is this. Are we to carry on with the old idea of private enterprise, with its right to cut its own throat and impoverish the country,

Aeronautics Act
or are we so far as air service is concerned, to inject into the whole set-up the principle of planning for the public interest? It seems to me that that is the difference between the powers of the board of transport commissioners and the powers of the air transport board which the minister proposes to establish. On the one hand you have what is really a judicial body. But here you will have rather a body whose purpose is to help the government formulate policy. As I understand it, if this bill becomes law and we go ahead with the government's proposal, the decision will have been made that so far as air service is concerned there is to be planning as a matter of government policy.
The minister a little while ago, in one of his replies to the hon. member for Lake Centre, stressed one point which I think needs to be stressed again and again when he spoke of the cost of developing airports, beams, ranges and all the other facilities that are necessary to flying. My friends to my right are continually singing the praises of private enterprise. Yet we know quite well that we would not have had aviation developed to the point it has reached to-day in this country if it had not been for the huge expenditures of public money on the facilities that are necessary to make flying possible. I insist that if it is going to require the expenditure of public money to provide the basic essentials of flying, the public, having a major interest in the whole set-up, has the right to expect the government to see to it that these services are properly planned.
A great deal is said about our concern for our young men of the air force who will come home well trained and capable of providing flying services all over Canada. I want to put in a word for them in this way. I feel that they should not come home to the kind of cut-throat experiences which this country had to undergo in the early days of flying, when sufficient government expenditure was not made available to make flying practicable and safe. The result was that pilots were rushing in wherever it was possible to make half a living, and eventually competition in those areas forced them all out. We have also had the story of private companies in this country culminating in the merger of a dozen or more companies in Canadian Pacific Air Lines. All of this, as I see it, adds up to the fact that if we do not have the regulation and planning of all our air transport services, our airmen in the Royal Canadian Air Force will come home to a set-up of cut-throat competition which will discourage and greatly disillusion them.
To me the history of the development of our air services in this country indicates
definitely that it does require the expenditure of public money and public planning. While, as I said before, I. am not satisfied that the government goes far enough, I am with the minister every inch of the way that he does go in this bill. As I said, I felt that the hon. member for Davenport was different from the previous speakers in that he did get down to the real issue, namely, the issue as between private enterprise and public control.
What is the hon. gentleman's idea with respect to the north and south feeder lines? Should they be taken over by the T.C.A. or be operated by private enterprise?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The difference between
the member for Lake Centre and ourselves is basically over the question whether air services are to be a matter of government policy or whether the government is simply to stand on the sidelines and allow private enterprise to have its own way. What we have here is not, as I see it, dictatorship but rather the extension of the principle of responsible government. What I was trying to say was that as between the minister and the governor in council having the authority it is six of one and half a dozen of the other, and it does not matter to me which it is; but as between the minister having any real say in the matter-the minister or the government, however you put it- and the government merely standing on the side as a judicial body and allowing private enterprise to go ahead and cut its own throat and do a disservice to the country at large, I am in favour of the matter being in the hands of the people.
Under this bill recommendations will be made to the government or to the minister which will involve the expenditure of money. You will have under the provisions of the bill not just a judicial body making decisions as between competing firms but a body making recommendations to the government for the development of airways, and that will involve the expenditure of public money; and once you introduce that element into it you are flying in the face of our whole concept of responsible government if you suggest that the minister or the government should not be responsible for any implementing of the decisions of the board. For that reason 1 think the bill is right when it puts this measure of authority, if you want to call it that, though I call it responsibility, in the hands of the minister.
I am not surprised that my hon. friends to the right find it difficult to understand
fMr. Knowles,]
this concept. What you have here is an attempt, as far as it goes, to avoid the kind of mistakes this country made when it first launched on the development of our railway systems. In this instance we know from the start that if there is to be a proper and adequate development of this tremendous means of modern transportation, air services, money will have to be provided by the people. It is the people's interests that are paramount, and I take the position, with the Minister of Munitions and Supply, that it should be under the direction and control of the people through their duly elected government.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre omitted to refer to the question of centralization of power at Ottawa, whereby neither the provincial governments nor an individual in those provinces will be able to go into the flying business unless he obtains a licence from and is controlled by some department at Ottawa. The hon. member centred his argument on the difference between private and public ownership. I came to the House of Commons in 1930, and I view with alarm the centralization of power in Ottawa. Canada is different from all other countries. It is perhaps four thousand miles in extent. It has great, areas sparsely settled. There is no country comparable to it, with the exception of the United States. It therefore behooves us to watch with a great deal of care-especially those of us who come from the east and the west-the powers which we think we are losing.

I am a little surprised at the attitude taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre with reference to the north and south feeder routes. If this policy is continued, and if the government insists that the railways shall be divorced from the air lines, only one thing can eventually happen. We shall have a complete

government monopoly on the across-Canada system and on the north and south feeder routes, because I believe it is impossible to carry on a system of small operating units all the way across the country, each one with separate overhead and with no means of coordination of cooperation between the whole.

I think it might be worth while to take a few moments to consider what the bill before the house entails. The bill amends the Aeronautics Act, which in turn was passed in 1918. It was the supreme law governing aviation in Canada until it was amended in 1938.
The claim is made that the minister is setting up a dictatorship. That has been said several times. Let me say that the effect of the amendments are to transfer many of the responsibilities of the minister to a -board. Previously under the act those were the sole responsibilities of the minister. The hon. member for Yale administered the Aeronautcs Act for four or five years; he was then the dictator of aviation in this country. I cannot believe that he was very uneasy aibout the situation, or that the country was very uneasy; nevertheless in those years no plane could be licensed in this country, no route could be flown and no person could be a pilot except under a certificate from the hon. member for Yale. No-w we are changing that in what direction? We are setting up a board which on its own initiative will be responsible for licensing and for a number of other functions formerly performed by the minister.
Let us see what the other criticism is.

Before the minister leaves that point, will he say what powers are taken away from him that he had under the Aeronautics Act? As I read that act there is only one change; that is in connection with the licensing of aircraft, and even it is made subject to the approval of the minister.
No; final authority in that regard is with the aeronautics board.
It says, "subject to the approval of the minister."

Let me make my speech; you have made several. In 1938 an attempt was made to do something in this direction; the board of transport commissioners were asked to perform certain functions that previously had been performed by the minister. That bill was brought in by this government and introduced by myself, as Minister of Transport. That provision was inserted in the act with the idea of strengthening the machinery in connection with the allocation of air routes

Aeronautics Act
and licensing. It has become obvious that unless the act is again changed, in future there will be only two airway systems in Canada; one, the publicly owned Trans-Canada system-and it will take some vigilance on the part of governments from time to time to maintain that system in its present state- and the other owned by another railway. Applications have been filed by the privately owned railway for every route that has been opened or suggested in Canada; and under the present act, if those routes were proclaimed the transport board might very logically assign them to the privately owned railway. The government has had to consider whether or not that would be a good thing. In other words should this government permit, in war time-and remember that the privately owned railway entered the aviation field and has built up its business in that field during the war years-the air of Canada to be preempted by two railway systems; should we sit idly by and let that happen? That is the decision we have had to make. Rightly or wrongly the government has decided that it is not in the best interests of Canada, not in the public interests, to allow that to happen. Therefore we are doing what has been done in other countries; we are asking surface transportation to divest itself of its interests in air transportation, and we are amending the Aeronautics Act accordingly.
I have stated some of the objections to having the air dominated by two railway systems. I have said that we did not wish to bring to the development of our airways the competitive methods adopted in building our surface transportation. Many hon. members of the house, who are young men, have never seen that competitive system in action. I happen to be one of the older men in the house, and I remember the methods employed when that competition was at its height. If hon. members wish to see how that scramble for franchises was carried on, let them look at the situation that exists to-day. If they wish to see a railroad propaganda machine in action, let them look about to-day. What has happened? Every Conservative paper in Canada has carried the statement that this is a personal matter with Mr. Howe, that his colleagues are not in agreement with him. That was the first statement, and I think it was carried in practically every Conservative paper. I deny it absolutely.

Then this has been represented as a step toward public ownership. Nothing of the kind is contemplated, or has been suggested, or is contained in any statement of government policy with regard to the air. What happened as far as Trans-Canada Air Lines was concerned? Private enterprise was asked to participate in the building of Trans-Canada Air Lines. At that time private enterprise did not care to participate, so that the system was developed as a government enterprise. The franchise was the gift of the people of Canada, and the government of the day decided to develop that franchise for the benefit of the people of Canada. The financial arrangements provided that increased earnings would be returned to the users of the system and to the public at large by way of reductions in the cost of carrying air mail. The system has been established. It had been in operation for only one year before war broke out, and has not been able to develop as rapidly as the requirements of the country have demanded. I think anyone interested in Canada's war effort will agree that the government could not reasonably have pressed the development of Trans-Canada Air Lines in preference to its war effort. However, it is the purpose of this government, as I hope it will be the purpose of succeeding governments, to protect the franchise of Trans-Canada Air Lines as a great public service. Trans-Canada
Aeronautics Act

Air Lines was not an invasion of private rights but the assumption of a public right. Until now the board of transport commissioners was a board to which such matters as licensing might be committed for examination. the individual is; the fact is that it is to be a minister. To my mind it would be much preferable that the minister's actions be curbed to the extent of examination by a board. At the risk of being termed a propagandist I should like to say a word or two in regard to the bill, not from a party standpoint at all, but as a citizen of Canada.
I do not thmk there can be any disagreement when I say that the measure before the committee has for its purpose the creation of a government monopoly in respect of air transport services. The terms of the measure go that far, and do in fact set up a government monopoly.
I understand this is a general discussion, but that section 1 is before the committee. Perhaps I might draw the attention of hon. members to the wording of section 12(1), which states:
Subject to the approval of the minister, the board may issue to any person applying therefor a licence to operate a commercial air service.
The words "to any person" have a very broad meaning. Reading that section of the measure alone, one would come to the conclusion that anyone applying could get a licence. However the next subsection says:
No such licence shall be issued in respect of a commercial air service owned, leased, controlled or operated by any person who is engaged in the transport of goods or passengers for hire or reward by means other than aircraft-
This, in effect, prohibits the railway companies from carrying on air transportation services. In my view that is not a good policy. I do not see why the issue of licences to transportation companies should be prohibited. Jt is my view that our two big railway companies, the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, are better equipped and better qualified to give transport services by air than are any other people or companies in Canada. I am not shocked by what the minister has described as two railway companies preempting air services in Canada. I think those two companies could very well be allowed and encouraged to preempt air service in this country, because they can carry it on so much better than any other institutions or organizations of which I know at the present time. The fact is that the Canadian National Railways have successfully operated Trans-Canada Air Lines, and that the Canadian Pacific Railway has successfully operated Canadian Pacific Air Lines. Why not let them carry on? These two companies have made a success of transportation, and this measure would exterminate their air transport activities. I do not see how it can be considered in the public interest to cancel their licences, to prohibit the renewal of licences or to prohibit issuing new licences to them. Such would be the effect of this measure.
The bill provides:
The board shall review all licences . . . and may cancel or suspend any such licence as it sees fit.
It has a free hand to cancel any licence it wishes, with or without cause. Even that, apparently, is not considered sufficiently extreme, because if those licences are not so cancelled, by the following section they cease to be valid at the termination of the war. In other words, the licences which now exist are exterminated by this measure.
It has been my experience that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways are giving the country a first-class air transport service. I know that the Canadian Pacific Air Lines is giving the west and the north country a splendid service. I cannot understand why the government should wish to discontinue that service when in fact it should be supported and encouraged.
