Those lines were given up for war reasons.

They were really given up before the war, because I was up there just at the beginning of the war. It was partly because of what I mentioned last night, the destruction of prospecting. Most of these air lines were serving the prospectors, the diamond drilling crews and the small mines. The first time I went into Siscoe the only way I could go was by air.
These companies made it possible for us to establish a world lead in the carriage of air freight. My objection to this bill is that it proscribes the operation of small companies like these. Under the regulations they would have to have definite routes. These companies did not have definite routes. In 1933, 1934 and 1935 there was a great deal of activity in the Chibougamou district in northwest Quebec. Several lines, at least General Airways, flew regular services from Noranda or Rouyn to Chibougamou andt they would stop to service diamond drilling crews operating in that district. Unfortunately the district did not live up to expectations. A great deal of money was spent but not a single producing mine waa

Aeronautics Act
developed. That illustrates the hazards of the mining business. General Airways ran a definite route and they sold a ticket, a printed contract. Naturally, when that area failed there was no reason to run aircraft into the district and the line was discontinued.
Under this legislation we would say that General Airways should have a monopoly into the Chibougamou district. However, Prospectors Airways, which was a mining and prospecting corporation, at one time was interested in the Chibougamou field. I did not fly with them, but I understand that they had a plane which serviced their operations in the district which was also serviced by General Airways. In my opinion there was no harm in that because both companies were endeavouring to develop the country. If you were interested in getting into the country you had the option of travelling on one or the other line. Prospectors Airways did not have a regular service but occasionally, I understand, they would take a passenger in.
This bill in its precise and limiting clauses is going to put a damper on the development of such lines as I have mentioned.
In what way?

Because each line will have a prescribed route; each line will have its individual destination point. In the development of the north country, which is what I am interested in, you cannot prescribe and limit the activities of aircraft or the men who fly them.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before six o'clock I was discussing briefly the operations of the small operators in Canada who are known as the bush pilots or bush fliers. I had dealt with a number of the smaller operations, particularly those from the mining centre of Rouyn and Noranda.
I should now like to discuss an operation on the Pacific coast which has been taken over by Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I refer to the operation which was known as the Ginger Coote Air Services. They flew from Vancouver to Victoria but chiefly from Vancouver to Port Alberni and to the Zeballos mining district. I think this operation had a world record for time saved by air. In the ordinary course of events, if you wanted to go to the Zeballos mining field you took a boat, and it took you between five and six days to go
from Vancouver around the end of Vancouver island, calling at a great number of ports on the way and lying over at night at some of them, but you could fly there by the Ginger Coote Air Services in two hours. You could get in there and back in a day quite easily. That was a saving, it has been estimated, particularly if the weather was at all bad, of twelve days, which I think is a record of time saved in travelling by air. It shows the vital part which these pioneer air services have played in the development of Canada. Ginger Coote has been taken over by the C.P.A. I think Ginger Coote could not make it go, although I am not sure, and the reason he could not was none other than that the Zeballos mining camp did not develop into a major camp. In the beginning this operator was prepared to go in there and take a chance on the development of this new field. This bill in its clauses will, I feel, militate against the small operators. Ginger Coote operated two Waco float planes. He took a chance on the Zeballo field developing into a major camp. The camp was all right for a few years and it may open again and probably will, but I understand that it is now completely closed down.
The reason why Canadian Pacific Air Lines took that service over was to provide an essential service. To-day they operate from Patricia Bay to Vancouver. I flew there just the other day myself. They are operating an essential service. If one wanted to charter a plane from them or from some other big corporation or to be flown north of the Zeballos field, I do not think you would be able to do so even if there was no war, because the big operators would allow no deviation from the regular routes of their aircraft.
Several other air services small in nature have more or less gone by the board. One of them was Patricia Airways. It flew into the Albany river territory in northern Ontario, the Patricia mine, the Pickle Crow mine and various other districts. Here again, if these fields did not develop into a major field, the small operator would find it difficult to continue. None of these operators was subsidized, as I remember. They just took a chance. They were the true pioneers, the ones to whom we have to be thankful for the leading position we occupied in world aviation in those critical years of the middle thirties. Most of these operators operated on a shoe-string. Their planes were not new. They were planes like the single-engined Stinson or the Fairchild or the Waco or even the De Havilland Moth. They operated on floats in the summer and skis in winter. They had a very interesting
Aeronautics Act

effect on the Canadian aircraft field, because out of this development came the only original Canadian aircraft, the Noorduyn Norseman. This aircraft was developed specifically 'to undertake the job of bush flying and it was extremely successful. In fact the Noorduyn Norseman is to-day, I understand, being used with very little alteration by all the united nations as a short haul float plane for freight and passengers. I understand that it has proved more successful than any other design. That was one of the advantages we had by developing the small operator and the bush flyer.
Let me say a word about the safety of these operators. We are very proud of the fact that Trans-Canada Air Lines has a unique record for safety, but what an extremely enviable record these old bush flyers had in their day. As far as I know, in all the operations from Noranda-and there would be as many as fifteen and sometimes twenty planes in and out that airport or little wharf every day- there was only one fatal accident, and on the Pacific coast there was, I believe, only one fatal accident which occurred near Fort Albemi on the forbidden plateau. When we think of the tremendous volume of freight and the tremendous development that was carried out by those men, with their record of safety, surely it is our first duty to see to it that whatever legislation we may pass or whatever legislation we may bring down in this house, the future of the small operator, the man who has one or two planes, the man who is perhaps operating a specialty service, who is operating where the big operators cannot go, is made secure; because he is the man, and that is the operation, that has built Canadian aviation. It was not the great transcontinental lines that made Canadian aviation, but the small operator operating with one or two planes, in the certain knowledge that if he had a crash he probably could not afford to buy another one. These were the men who developed aviation and these are the men we seem to have forgotten. We have got into our heads a grandiose idea about transcontinental and transatlantic aviation. This is all very important in its way, but we must remember that Canada is still a pioneer country and that if we are to develop, as I hope we shall, it is to the pioneer operator that we still have to look. While it is all very well to consider the transcontinental service and to have pictures of pretty stewardesses tripping about and soothing the brow of the tired businessman-
Or cabinet minister.

-we must remember that it is the hobnail-booted prospector and engi-

neer who is going to fill the needs of industry and make the payroll that will meet the requirements of the future. These are things we are apt to forget. We get delusions of grandeur, and that is one of the reasons why I object to the restrictive clauses in this bill. When clause 12 comes up I hope to have something more to say on it.

I have been following all the legislation brought down by the minister, and I thought it might be wise, in view of the remarks made by my colleague, the hon. member for Lake Centre, this afternoon with reference to recourse to the law, and also having regard to the remarks made by the minister to-day, to remind the committee of something that is very interesting, but something that this government has forgotten. The 15th of June was a date which meant a great deal to the British people, for on that date 729 years ago the barons of England gathered at Runnymede outside Windsor to meet King John. It was on that day that absolute power of the state, held through the person of the king, was compelled to yield to the rule of law and the rights of man. This was set down in the great charter, magna charta. It is still a symbol of freedom, so highly appraised and carefully cherished, that the document itself was sent to Washington for safe-keeping during the blitz. The rule of law!
All that my hon. friend the member for Lake Centre asks is that the rule of law shall be observed; access to the law in order to redress grievances must be made as easy as possible. How far we are getting away from that easy access to the law in the legislation we have had put before us this session! So far as I can see, the minister wants to make appeals to the courts as difficult as he can. This afternoon he said: Let anyone who wants a licence to operate start an airways company; if he can get it let him start one. How ridiculous that is. Who in the world is going to go to the expense of starting an airways company with all the expenditures attached thereto, the purchase of aeroplanes, equipment and all that sort of thing, with all the uncertainty of law that is inseparable from the venture? The request of the hon. member for Lake Centre is very reasonable.
What is the position of my hon. friends to the left, the socialist party? They say: "Go ahead, you young fellows, when you get back. Get busy and start out in the aeroplane business and work it all up, and the moment you begin to make a profit out of it we will take it over. We will confiscate it." That is what they say.

Aeronautics Act

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is what the Canadian Pacific Railway Company did.

The Canadian Pacific did nothing of the kind. My hon. friend does not know what he is talking about when he says that. The C.P.R., as a matter of fact, took over some of these companies and have some of these fellows working with them on shares, and the hon. member knows that. Are there to be no vested interests in this country? Is the man in the corner grocery store to be secure in his job when he gets busy and builds up a business that is worth while? Who is going to venture in this great Canada of ours with the opportunities we have, in face of that sort of thing? Who. is going to develop the country if, after he has got something started that begins to be . profitable, our national socialist friends to the left take it all away from him? Who is going to venture? Who is going to develop without the security of magna charta? Too much power is being vested in this government. Access to the courts is getting more difficult all the time. To-day the minister said: Let them start in business, with all the expenses attached to it, and then see if they can get a licence to do it. I wish to point out that our democracy was founded on the danger of absolute power. This is not government of the people, for the people, by the people. There is danger of absolute power. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that the taste of power in war time has gone to the heads of this government. They have to get back to peace-time legislation and function as a government ought to function. The people have been satisfied to be regimented and all that kind of thing in war time, but we shall never get any place in this country unless we have individual effort and enterprise. I say that history has repeated itself. It was ever thus in war time, and how! I ask the minister to reconsider his decision and in this legislation make access to the courts easier and remember magna charta.

This afternoon the minister said he was amazed that this bill had met with such a storm of propaganda. I was amazed that he should have described the criticism of this bill as a storm of propaganda. I think his remarks contain certain innuendoes and implications that should not be allowed to go unchallenged.
I do not think the minister would charge the Winnipeg Free Press with indulging in a storm of propaganda, but, sir, that newspaper has been very critical of some of the provisions of this bill. I have before me a copy of an editorial that appeared in that paper on April 11 last, after the minister had set forth
the policy of the government in this house. I do not propose to read all the editorial, but in it I find this statement:
One feature of Mr. Howe's speech, however, requires far more explanation than it has yet got. That is the determination on the government's part to divorce air and rail transportation. Why? What good purpose is being served? All that we have from Mr. Howe is the flat statement that he believes it wise. But that is not good enough.
This is not Conservative propaganda or Conservative criticism; it is an editorial from the Winnipeg Free Press. The editorial goes on to say:
Many reasons can be put forward for maintaining air and rail connections. The services in certain respects are complementary, and_ it-is obvious that important economies in operation can be obtained by a sharing of certain costs. On this point there must be definite suspension of judgment until the case for separation is more clearly defined.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association is a large and important organization in this country. Its members are citizens of Canada who have played an important part in the industrial development of the dominion and who have done an important job during this war. After this bill was before the committee last, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association presented a submission, a copy of which I presume the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who is acting as Minister of Transport, has received. I have this submission before me. I am tempted to read it all, but I shall not do so. Here is one paragraph that I shall read to the committee:
The long experience gained through the administration of existing legislation pertaining to transportation regulation has proven that the administrative board to deal adequately and fairly with various statutory conditions must be clothed with adequate powers and staffed with experienced and expert personnel. Only in this way can all concerned be assured of fair and independent action on matters dealt with by such board. The conditions of Bill 133 fall far short from meeting this important test.
I do not think either the Winnipeg Free Press or the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, of which perhaps the minister was at one time a member-
Do not accuse me of that.
Does the minister deny it.
Perhaps he still is a member.

I do not think it can be described as indulging in a storm of propaganda when it criticizes the provisions of this bill.
When this bill was introduced in the house earlier this session the Minister of Munitions
Aeronautics Act

and Supply said that in general it followed the provisions of the Aeronautical Act of the United States and the functions of the civil aeronautics authority. But there are wide differences between the United States act and the bill before us. The only apparent parallels are minor details. The differences between the United States act and this bill are wide both in particular and in fact.
The civil aeronautics board of the United States consists of five members. The act provides that not more than three of them shall be of the same political party. It functions independently of the secretary of commerce. It reports directly-
Where did that information come from?
-to the president and to congress. This bill provides that the report shall be made to the Minister of Transport. The United States act does not do that.
Each reports to the government.

Under the United States act the report is made directly to the president and to congress. The bill before us provides for but three members. There are no legal restrictions as to political affiliations, and the board is directly under the authority of the minister, whom it advises and whose directions it executes.
There is perhaps only one respect in which the United States act and this bill are similar. Under our bill and under the United States act a surface carrier cannot engage in air transport, but I believe that the minister was inadequately informed when he stated in this house that he knew of no other country where the control of aviation was in the hands of surface carriers. The most striking example to contradict that statement is to be found in Great Britain, where the internal air services are operated by railway companies and where steamship companies already are making plans, apparently with the informal encouragement of the government, to operate external services-to other countries after the war. For some reason we have adopted the policy of the United States rather than that of Great Britain. I fail to understand under what principle you can enact legislation providing that a corporation must confine its activities to one phase or aspect of its business.
A fundamental difference between the United States act and the bill we have before us is to be found in the principle of a monopoly, publicly owned or otherwise.

against that of competition where feasible. We have created an instrument for our air policy in Trans-Canada Air Lines, and have given it wide, exclusive rights. I do not object to that. If the government of this country want to establish a sole air line from the Atlantic to the Pacific they have a perfect right to do so, having entered the field first. But, the civil aeronautics act of the United States explicitly requires that no exclusive right shall be granted for the use of any civil airway, and that no certificate shall confer any proprietary or executive rights in the use of any air space, civil airway, airport or air navigation facilities. Our bill would prevent competition in the Canadian air. The United States act permits competition in the Unted States "to the extent necessary to assure the sound development of an air transportation system properly adapted to the needs of the foreign and domestic commerce of the United States." If you refer to the sections of the United States act which I have mentioned you will see that our bill does not follow the provisions of the United States act except in minor details.
We have objected to the great powers given the minister under this bill. We have objected to the power to make regulations. We have objected to the fact that the minister, who makes decisions in the first place, should sit as a court of appeal on his own decisions. The minister has resented our criticism. This afternoon he said that a brand new party name was becoming completely unstuck, and that the word "Progressive" should be dropped. As I have said before, Mr. Chairman, under our system of democratic government it is the duty of members of this house to make the laws, while it is the duty of independent judges to interpret and enforce those laws. If it is unprogressive to insist on that principle being observed, then this party is unprogressive. If it is progressive to insist that we have a dictatorship set up in this country, then this party is unprogressive.
I have a great many suspicions and fears when I read in a bill that a minister, or the governor in council, has the right to make regulations. If these regulations are of a purely administrative nature there may not be much objection, but the difficulty and danger arise from the fact that in too many cases these regulations are really laws which impose penalties. I remember that two or three years ago, I think perhaps it was in 1940 or 1941, the Minister of Fisheries with the approval of the governor in council made a regulation. It appeared very simple; it was known as special regulation No. 9, and pro-

Aeronautics Act
vided that there should be no net fishing in the non-tidal waters of the Saint John river without a permit from the minister. No permits were granted, and the result was that this order in council took away the riparian rights people had in the non-tidal waters of the Saint John river. They lost their propertj' without receiving any compensation therefor. That wrong has never been redressed, but one of these days that will have to be done. So that I think I am justified in being suspicious of the provisions of these acts which allow tire governor in council to pass regulations, about which the members of this house have no say and which have the force of law. It is our duty in this house to make the laws; they should not be made by regulation or order in council except in war time.
We have objected to the provision of this bill which allows the minister to sit as a court of appeal after he has given a decision in the first place. I think it was the hon. member for Cape Breton South who, in speaking on the bill this afternoon, said that this measure was bringing back prerogatives which should remain with the house. It is doing nothing of the kind; it is taking away prerogatives that should remain in this house. It is taking away the rights of hon. members to make the laws of the country. That is one of the reasons for which their constituents elected them. There is a principle of natural justice involved, one which may not be found in any book of law, to the effect that no man should be judge in his own cause. But here, under this measure, we have the minister first deciding whether or not a man should have a licence. The minister has to pass on that first; then if the man feels he has not been fairly treated, or if he has some grievance, he has the right of appeal. To whom does he appeal? Why, he appeals to the minister, the man who makes the decision in the first instance. I say that violates a principle of natural justice, and it is not a position which hon. members should be asked to accept in any bill.
Under this measure tremendous powers are given to the minister. In November of last year the board of trade of Halifax and the board of trade of Saint John made a joint application to have an air line established between those two cities. There was great need for a service of that kind, because there is a good deal of business carried on between those two points. Many members of our armed forces are stationed at one or other of the cities, and at times they have occasion to move quickly between those two points. Although a joint application was made by those two boards of trade, it was refused. The
refusal was made, despite the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway company was prepared to institute a service immediately-a good service, with proper machines.
I have heard some criticism of the Canadian Pacific, but may I say right here that that railway has rendered great service to the port of Saint John. It has been largely through the efforts of the Canadian Pacific that we have a port there at the present time, and were it not for that railway I do not know where Saint John would be to-day. We are deeply indebted to that great corporation.
I put a question on the order paper in connection with this matter. It is to be found at page 781 of Hansard, and is in these words:
Is it the intention of the government to establish an air service between Saint John, New Brunswick, and Halifax, Nova Scotia, and if so, when will the service commence to operate?
The answer I received was as follows:
Trans-Canada Air Lines has been authorized by order in council P.C. 6256 of August 6, 1943, made pursuant to the "Trans-Canada contract" authorized under the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act, 1937, to establish a service between Blissville, New Brunswick, and Halifax, which will be placed in operation immediately upon the completion of a radio range now under construction at an intermediate aerodrome on the route between Saint John and Halifax.
I understand that service is to be established at an early day, although I do not know just when. I have not seen the announcement.

Well, then, it was established on July 1 of this year. I wish to add, however, that in my opinion that service is going to be absolutely inadequate and unsatisfactory. Hon. members may not know where Blissville is, but for their information may I say it is situated in the county of Sunbury, about forty-four miles from Saint John. Forty-four miles is not a great distance, when one visualizes a modern, first-class paved road. But a great part of the road to Blissville is only a secondary road. Not only is it a country road, but it is one on which there are sharp curves anad steep hills. I doubt if a road of that kind can be kept open in the winter. I should think-and I may be exaggerating a little when I say this-that possibly it would take almost as long to go from Blissville to Saint John by motorcar as to go from Halifax to Saint John by air. The situation, so far as Saint John is concerned, is absolutely out of the question. Time will prove whether I am right or wrong, but my suggestion is that a better and more convenient location should be established, because aircraft landing at
Aeronautics Act

Blissville are much farther from Saint John than they should be. I was going to say that it would be a two-hour drive from the airport to the city; when I say that I may be exaggerating a little. But the fact is that it is a long distance away. I am satisfied1 that the situation will prove most unsatisfactory and inadequate.

With reference to the service at Blissville, might I point out that, unfortunately, it is not possible to land large aircraft unless a standard landing field is available. The longest runway of the aerodrome at Saint John is about 2,000 feet, ending in a rock pile. It is not possible to land modern transport aircraft in that aerodrome. In order to give Saint John aeroplane service, it was necessary to use the nearest suitable field, and that happened to be at Blissville. Blissville is on the main line of Trans-Canada Air Lines, and is situated about halfway between Saint John and Fredericton. Until a suitable field can be provided at Saint John, that field will be used. The new service will be the means of bringing the mails to Saint John several hours more quickly than could be arranged by the recent air mail route.
My hon. friend says that it will take as long to go to the airport from Saint John as to go from Blissville to Halifax. Perhaps that is true. It takes as long to drive from the centre of Montreal to Montreal airport as it takes to go from Montreal airport to Ottawa. Despite that fact, there is a great deal of traffic by air between Montreal and Ottawa. Both the Toronto and Montreal airports are well located, when compared with airports of other large cities. I might add that the distance from Toronto to Mai ton is about twenty-two miles; yet there is heavy travel from Malton airport.
I am not suggesting that the final word has been said respecting an airport for Saint John. Plans are now under way to develop an airport which will be more suitable so far as its distance from the city is concerned. But, as I said earlier, it is impossible to divert labour from war work or other essential work, to undertake a purely peace-time project. We believe the service now being offered at Saint John, through Blissville, is a considerable advance over the air mail service which has been enjoyed in the past. We regard it as a step toward a still more adequate service in the future.
Will the minister say whether there is any locational difficulty in connection with developing Toronto airport as a major airport, if the runways were built long enough?
Toronto airport?
Toronto island airport.

That is in the middle of a nest of very high buildings. Within half a mile there are high buildings like the Royal York hotel, as well as two grain elevators. If my hon. friend thinks a pilot would enjoy going in there on a rainy evening with twenty or thirty passengers back of him, he is very much mistaken.
Even if the runways were enlarged?

Even if the runways were two miles long I do not think any pilot would undertake to make a blind landing at Toronto island. If an airport is not suitable for bad weather, it is not suitable at all, because passengers must know in advance the airport that will be their point of arrival or departure.
I have seen T.C.A. planes fly from there.
I have flown into and out of it many times, but always in good weather.

Mr. Chairman, we on this side of the house believe that there is a very important principle at stake, and we have endeavoured to place our viewpoint before the minister on this and previous occasions. This bill, amongst other things, provides for the setting up of a board. While the minister in his interview with Canadian Aviation magazine has stated that the board will exercise judicial functions, as the bill is at present it will simply be a stooge or pawn in the hands of the minister.
The application of this legislation will be mainly confined to the after the war period. If the principle enunciated by the minister is followed out, the granting of licences will be held back until after the war in order to assure an opportunity being given to our men returning from overseas to secure some of these licences. If this bill goes through in its present form we feel that it will stifle and strangle the expansion of air development in this country. It will place everyone who desires to expand in the way of air development subject, not to the regulations or orders of a judicial body, but to the approval of the minister in everything that is done. Over and over again the minister has repeated by way of explanation that this board is similar to the civil aeronautics authority in the United States. The hon. member for St. John-Albert has shown that one similarity is that the civil aeronautics authority in the United States has the-

Aeronautics Act
power to make regulations and control, but that board has the power to exercise judicial functions also and to make decisions as between individuals, untrammeled' and unfettered by the executive.

My hon. friend is quite wrong. Licences for air lines are not issued by the aeronautics board; they are issued by the President of the United States, who is the executive in that country, just as the cabinet in Canada is the executive in this country.
That is true enough, but the determination is made by the board.
It is a recommendation by the board.

The recommendation is accepted; it is in no case refused. That is the difference between these boards in one particular. Surely, with the coming of- peace we in this parliament have the right to assure once more the return to democratic principles and not permit the power of any official to be uncontrolled. We must assure that opportunity is given to aggrieved individuals to have recourse to the courts in order to secure justice. Under this board as it is to be set up under this bill there is not an individual or a company who, having been unfairly treated, will have any recourse whatsoever.
I mentioned a while ago the desire of the province of Ontario to establish air lines, and the minister said that the matter could be determined by the board, but official determination will rest with the minister. I asked him the simple question whether or not he would agree in principle, whether or not he would say it is right and proper that any provinces-not only the province of Ontario- should be permitted to operate air lines within their boundaries, but he neglected to give his ideas thereon. He has been very free with his ideas as to certain principles that will guide this board and the minister, but when it comes to a question such as the one I asked there is grave uncertainty in the answer given thereto.
If this board is set up as outlined in the bill, equality under the law will be denied. There was equality under the law between 1938 and the present time, subject, of course, to the exigencies of war as set out in the order in council that was passed in 1940 or 1941. All we are asking for is that all shall have an equal opportunity. We have no interest in the matter of monopolies. The minister says that this bill is similar to the act in the United States, but in this bill there is no such provision that would deny monopoly as exists
in the act of the United States. Under that act when an application is made for a certificate, publication is made of the application. Public notice is given thereof and any interested person may file a protest.
What is even more important, that act provides that no transfer of service will be allowed unless approved by the board as being consistent with public interest. Finally there can be no merger of air carriers except when approved by the authority. I find it difficult to follow the minister in his peregrinations since he made his first declaration of policy. When he first declared his policy he said that the railway and shipping companies shall not operate airways, that both T.C.A. and C.P.A. would have to divorce themselves from the railway companies to which they belonged. He said that that was imperative, and indicated that that was one reason for this legislation. As time went on, he changed his viewpoint considerably for in an interview with Canadian Aviation, he said:
I call your attention to the fact that C.P.A. has not been ordered to break up its system. The statement of government policy indicated that air lines will be separate operations from surface transportation.
And a little later on:
There is nothing to prevent C.P.A. from continuing its present operations under other than railway ownership.
As the bill is brought down there is no such imperative provision as at first enunciated by the minister. The provision is that no licence shall be issued to any such company or person unless the governor in council is of opinion that it is in the public interest that such licence be issued. That is a long way along the road from the declaration which was made when the minister first announced his policy.
All that I want done is to assure that there shall be fairness in the distribution of these air licences. All I want to be assured of is that there shall be no discrimination against any person, that all shall be equally and fairly treated, and that no arbitrary power shall remain in the minister. This bill is not to take effect in the main until after the war. It may not be the present minister who will then be in charge. But the principle is there, Mr. Chairman, the principle that if we pass this bill as it is now, we shall be setting up a body having all the appearances of power, but denied the exercise of that power excepting subject to the minister. Under the former act that covered rail transportation, ocean transportation and air transportation, provision was made for appeal.
Aeronautics Act
An appeal on what?
The minister says, "an appeal on what?" An appeal on questions of jurisdiction or on questions of law.
Appeal on questions of law to the courts, and appeal on questions of jurisdiction to the cabinet.

The minister had better read the Railway Act and bring himself up to date. I have a copy of the act here.
I am going to ask the minister, will he accept an amendment providing that an appeal shall lie from the board to the Supreme Court of Canada upon a question of law or upon a question of jurisdiction, or both, upon leave therefor having been obtained from a judge of the said court upon application made within one month after the making of the order, decision, rule or regulation sought to be appealed from? There is nothing unreasonable in that. It will preserve as a principle that the subject shall not be subject to the dictatorial decisions of any person and be denied the right of recourse to the courts. That provision has been in the law for years. Is there any reason why it should be removed now? Has any circumstance occurred, within the past four years indicating that the transport board has not efficiently discharged its responsibility in accordance with law?
There was a suggestion here to-day from the hon. member for Cape Breton South that franchises had been granted for airways since 1938 on improper considerations. That was the import of the statement made by the hon. member, and I am going to ask the minister if there was any foundation for that statement, for it leaves a suggestion against the board of transport commissioners that, if unjustified, should be removed by the minister.
We on this side of the house believe that wTe ought not to confer authority by legislation upon any individual or any board the power, not only to make decisions that affect the future welfare of this country, but to interpret the decisions that they make without assuring the right to the individual aggrieved recourse to the courts.
During the period of the war we have accepted the principle that authoritarian decisions might be made by persons which deny the right of recourse and the right of review by the courts of this land. I cannot see why we should carry this principle into the days of peace ahead. Why should we by legislation in this parliament confirm for the future that

which members on all sides of this house have condemned as dangerous even in war time? We in this parliament have a great responsibility and I make this appeal to the minister in all seriousness. We have seen very recently how the rights and privileges of parliament can be infringed upon when freedom of speech in parliament has been punished and penalized outside parliament. For the first time since 1764 parliament has permitted a member of parliament to be punished for the exercise of the undoubted right of members of parliament to the exercise of freedom of speech without complaint. All these things, unless we object to them, are leading along a road that tend to make parliament merely a debating society.
For the minister to accept the right of appeal that I suggest and that other hon. members here have suggested will in no way interfere with the principle of the bill or with the enunciation of the policies to be followed by the government, but it will ensure fairness and justice to the individual. I never was more serious in any matter that has come before this parliament. I have objected to orders in council multiplying at a rate never before equalled in any parliament anywhere

in this country to-day eight times as many as have been passed in Great Britain since the war. We have accepted their intended use for the period of war in the interests of victory, in the interests of survival. But I submit that now, when we believe that the day of peace approaches, we should make it a point to put a stop to the continuation of the trend.
The suggested amendment does not interfere with the principle of the bill. If it is accepted the government may go ahead and carry out whatever its policy may be, as carry it out it will. But there will be assured to everyone an opportunity to equality before the law and the denial of the right of any group to determine rights in the absence of the individual, without regard to jurisdiction and without regard to law.
There is one other matter and I am through. When our men come back from overseas, after their training in aviation, we must assure that there will be available to at least a considerable percentage of them an opportunity to secure employment in this country. Only recently the administrator of civil aeronautics, Mr. Charles Stanton, speaking at Washington, stated his belief with regard to American aviation in the future. He said:
Aviation must be brought to every sizable community that has need of it. . . . We are now on the threshold of a great and intensive development requiring expansion along . every line, and in speaking of expansion, I do not

Aeronautics Act
mean adding a few more schedules from point to point, or just a few hundred miles of new routes each year. In speaking of expansion, I mean hundreds of new schedules, and thousands of miles of new routes, carrying millions of new passengers, and great quantities of air express, and practically all of the first-class mail.
We in Canada are not ready for this expansion. The Aeronautical Institute of Canada has given a great deal of study to this matter, and I should like to have a statement from the minister regarding the representations it has made concerning the question of'develop-ment of airfields at this time, to make ready for extended air facilities after the war. In the submission that was made it was pointed out:
In our war effort we are creating two gigantic reservoirs of education. In the factories we are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars training aircraft mechanics in the construction and servicing of aircraft. In the air force we are spending millions for the training of riggers, fitters, administrative and air personnel. We wish to use these reservoirs of education for the benefit of the nation at large.
There are in Canada 580 cities, towns and villages with a population in excess of 1,000 and only thirty-two of these places to-day have airmail passenger service. After the war is over, having regard to present developments, seventy-five more will be in that position, but there will be 470 of these towns and cities in Canada with no suitable airport or aviation facilities. We are concerned with rehabilitation under this measure-the rehabilitation of the men who return after service in the air force. For the expenditure at the present time of $20,000,000, airfields in these towns and cities, sufficient for post-war interurban aviation, could be developed, and the result would be that, when the war is over, if we had 400 or more airports ready we would be able to assure many hundreds of these returning airmen of an opportunity to go into business for themselves and to operate trunk services and interurban services between these cities and towns.
I often think of the difficulties that we shall have when peace comes. There are some
200,000	men in the air force, and at the very best, according to the highest estimates to-day, not more than 25,000, including groundcrew, will secure employment under the air scheme as formulated for the future. For the expenditure of $20 million, which is less than it now costs to train 800 airmen, we woidd set up in this country the foundation for a great and extensive Canadian air service which would assure, according to the estimates that I have received, about 60,000 men returning from overseas of an opportunity to carry on the work for which they have been trained and
educated, and in addition to that the demands for aeroplanes would result in the improvement of the aeroplane industry and would assure at least that portion of those to-day engaged in aeroplane production being carried on the payroll after the war.
I consider this to be the attitude of all members in this house toward this bill. We may disagree in the details, but our purpose is to ensure that in the foundation we now lay for aviation after the war we shall see to it that provision is made for maximum employment of the men who return, while at the same time we contribute to the welfare of the dominion. It is in that spirit that I have spoken, and I am asking the minister once more to advise the committee whether he can see his way clear to accept the amendment, or to introduce an amendment himself, in order to provide for equality in the administration of this vast undertaking- equality for all who apply, including the men who will be returning from overseas.

My hon. friend has proposed a most innocuous amendment. He proposes making provision in the bill for an appeal, in matters of law and jurisdiction, to the Supreme Court of Canada, to be granted on application to a judge of that court. That has been in the Transport Act, which is a very bulky document, since the act was 'drawn, and it has been acted upon very infrequently, if at all. I have no objection whatever to putting it in this bill, although what the question of jurisdiction or law has to do with this measure, which covers three pages of printed matter, I cannot imagine. The mountain has laboured and has brought forth a mouse, but if it is at all valuable we will put it in the bill.

The mouse has
remained in the statute books for the last thirty years.

But not in this act.
My hon. friend went on to say that the government was doing nothing about building airports for post-war aviation. Perhaps I could give a few figures on that. For all civilian airports up to the beginning of the war, the federal government has spent $16,240,550.83. That is for the building of aerodromes and radio facilities, and that figure includes S3,707,310.52 in grants to assist municipalities. Since the war began, the government has invested in airfields and radio facilities the sum of $141,184,827.40. That does not include buildings but is simply for aerodromes and radio facilities. That amount has been expended on improving sixty-four aerodromes

Aeronautics Act

and bringing them up to the standard required for modern aviation, and in building 147 new aerodromes.
How many of these are used for war purposes?
I did not say that.

As I understood my hon. friend, twenty million dollars will provide 200 more aerodromes. That is a very reasonable price for aerodromes in this day and generation. Well, my experience is that the average aerodrome costs between $2 and $3 million. Perhaps we shall not place too much reliance on the figures put out by the Aeronautics Institute of Canada. It is not a representative body of Canadian aviation in any sense of the word. I do not know that I need to say anything further. Now that we have accepted this Conservative amendment in a spirit of cooperation, I hope that we shall get cooperation and perhaps get on with this bill.

I do not wish to hold up the bill, but I do not agree with the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and I am impressed with the excellent remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre. I think this bill strikes at the very root of one of the vital necessities for post-war employment, post-war development and progress in general. It strikes at the very heart of individual enterprise, freedom of vocation and all those old principles that the great party which now forms the government once stood for. In fact, I can well recall when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was criticized for defending the laissez-faire-ism that has characterized Liberalism in Canada for the last quarter of a century and up until quite recently.
Since we appear to be approaching the end of this gigantic struggle overseas, I can see no one line of activity in this dominion that offers newer and fresher opportunity for the recently developed skill and ingenuity of so many thousands of our boys who are to-day fighting overseas. It has often been said that, despite all the terrors and difficulties of war, we can make more progress in the five awful years of war than we sometimes can in

fifty years of peace. It is unfortunate that we cannot speed up progress in time of peace. Like the mother of invention, necessity speeds it in war time. We have observed that in the two great wars of the last quarter of the century untold progress has been made. Whether it has been made from necessity, or from the marshalling of forces and the genius, skill and mentalities of all our people, it is not for me to say.
We find that this bill offers a curtailment. Indeed, it may well be accepted by many of our people as an indication of the trend of the times, a trend that may well be feared. As the hon. member for Lake Centre has well said, in time of war we accept certain regimentation; we are ready to endure certain restrictions. We are ready to accept and are, indeed, enduring licences to operate, licences to do business. We find that this bill passes the powers and prerogatives of the government on to the minister himself. I can think of no activity for which our young men would be more eager than civil aviation because of their experience in this war. I can think of no vocation that they would be more eager to enter into than the wide and great possibilities of air transportation in this dominion. From day to day we read in magazines what the helicopter will do and how it will be a subsidiary of the great Trans-Canada Air Lines. We can visualize the possibilities of the manufacture of those important modern airships, their servicing, the personnel to run them, and where it will fill in a great gap to encourage the consumption of manufactured goods to make up for the great destruction that is now taking the products of our toil.
The minister has said that he does not propose to allow the vigorous competition that we had in transportation systems of this country to continue. Since when, Mr. Chairman, has competition ceased to be the life of trade?
Where do you find anything in this bill that stops competition?

It is the prerogative of the minister to stop it or start it. This strange bill gives the minister power to grant licences. This bill gives him power to tell those who have a licence whether they can or cannot operate. The board of transport commissioners cannot do that; it is the minister. The minister has power to determine whether or not they can engage in business. If that does not prevent those who would like to go into this promising field of industrial activity from doing so, then I do not know what kind of bill could be passed that could frighten

Aeronautics Act
initiative any more. I consider that the minister could have improved this bill a great deal. As the hon. member for Lake Centre has said, I should like to see the minister reconsider some of these clauses. I should like him to reconsider the clause that says an appeal can be made only to the minister. It seems almost unnecessary to make provision for an appeal to the only person who can grant a licence. I realize that in the post-war period and in the period between war and peace the greatest caution must be exercised. I agree that we must have a board of commissioners. We must have a licence and a charter to operate a service, but it seems strange that only those who are prohibited in advance are those who are the most experienced in this operation.
We are told that the Trans-Canada Air Lines shall be given licences for any further routes that they may need in order to carry out their present agreements. If this is in keeping with the policy of enterprise and free individual initiative that my hon. friends have always proclaimed as their policy, I do not think any party or any government in this country has ever had a mandate from our people to change so fundamentally the principles of control over enterprise. It is true that we may have it in time of war, but we are here planning for peace time. I believe in the same old competition that was the lifeblood of trade all down through the years, rivalry, struggle and competition, whether it is with reference to the people in transportation or with reference to manufactured goods or to whatever it may be.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Especially in the thirties.

My hon. friend always harps back. I am not much concerned with those who live amid the antiquities of the past and dream of the old socialism that has come down through the years since Karl Marx. Evidently my hon. friend has no conception of what constitutes the lifeblood of industry in this country. I might refer my hon. friend to a period even farther back, during the last war, when the same line of thought which he and his party propound in this house seemed to capture the imagination of the Britishers, and they nationalized the coal mines. What happened? Under public ownership production dropped from 258 tons per man per year to 176 tons per man per year. They became alarmed when production steadily decreased under this government monopoly, as it might be called, and later on returned the coal mines to private industry, to those who had experience in operating them, and production went back up
100-291i
to 358 tons per year per man. But that experiment cost the government of Britain over $200,000,000.
I realize it may be said that this is not entirely a matter of public ownership, but at least it is a step in that direction. I do not know whether this step is being taken in view of the coming election. I know there are grumblings in the mulberry bushes these days, and much concern as to what might happen.
Are you in the bushes?

No, but my hon. friend will be in the bushes after the next election. I am surprised that my old laissez-faire champions, who used1 to say, " We stand for free enterprise, for equal opportunities for all," are now, on the eve of an election, terrified by the signs of the times, entering into a shotgun marriage with those who would destroy industry and bring in public ownership all along the line. Under this bill the minister will be free to do whatever he pleases. Someone said this afternoon that the Minister of Munitions and Supply had been a capable engineer. That is very true, and I do not say this because he is not in the chamber at the moment; but before he became a member of this government he engineered some of the finest buildings in this country. He did so under individual enterprise and initiative, and built great monuments to his technique and skill. I am, however, surprised to find a bill like this coming from such a skilful engineer. The minister alone can issue licences, but the board which is to be set up can cancel them without his approval. The minister can indicate the companies that will get all the licences they wish, and he can indicate in advance the companies that will not get licences. He can say, " Those of you who have had experience in operating air lines must stay out of this," with the exception of one line. I hope this skilful efigineer is not engineering a socialistic gesture toward my socialist friends to the left, because this bill offers very little encouragement or assurance to the maintenance of individual enterprise. Is this to be the encouragement offered to those who propose to develop the great resources of this country in order to provide employment for our people following this war? Is this to be the new doctrine, the new type of policy that is to encourage them? Are we to have a continuation of the present bureaucratic control? Are we to have a continuation of the restraint of trade, the regimentation, the licensing and so on? My hon. friend says that it is not a restraint of trade. Well, you might just as well restrain trade if you are going to restrain initiative.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Restraint of trade has always been the gospel of you and your party.
Well, my hon. friend restrained some of it, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That was your grand cure.

I can well remember how trade was restrained during the regime of hon. members opposite. My hon. friends always like to go back to the thirties, but I am trying to point out what may happen in the fifties. As an hon. member behind me says, hon. gentlemen opposite are like infants crying in the night, crying with a small voice in the face of the coming election. Hon. members opposite are very good at pointing to the thirties, no matter what issue is under discussion. Let me take my hon. friends back a little farther, if they want to talk about the past. Go back to the years from 1921 to 1929, before some hon. gentlemen oDposite were in this house. Why did the nur ber of people leaving this country exceed the natural increase? Why did so many people from Canada settle in the United States during those years? Why should there be more people from the province of Quebec living in the New England states than are living in Quebec to-day? Why were hon. gentlemen opposite dusting off their old free trade doctrine? Why were they saying of other policies, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre is saying to-night, "Because it is a Tory doctrine we shall have nothing to do with it." Why did they tinker with the tariff between elections, as they are starting to tinker with it again? Why should our artisans, our mechanics, the graduates of our universities, go to the United States, where they have remained until this day?
Order. This has nothing to do with civil aviation.

I am only answering the questions that are put to me. If it is in order for hon. gentlemen opposite to utter gibes in relation to what happened ten years ago, surely I am in order when I remind them of what happened in the ten years before that. The great depression they are talking about did not follow immediately after the last war; it followed immediately after the regime of the Liberal government, from 1921 to 1929, when every elevator in the country was full of unsold grain, and when millions of people left this country looking for jobs.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Civil aviation!
It would take some aviation to find the men and women who left this country because you denied them opportunities at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: What did you do in 1932?
In 1932 we were cleaning up the mess you left in 1929, and I have no apologies to offer in that connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: You ruined aviation for ten years.

Throughout the world there were thirty million people idle in 1932, and what happened in other countries from that year until 1940? The people, who, were starving and on relief according to the hon. gentleman opposite, enjoyed a higher standard of living than many of those employed in other countries, as we pointed out. Following the war this country will offer great opportunities, in aviation and in industrial development generally, if only we keep our feet on the ground and bear in mind our great traditions, not alone those of this party but also those of hon. gentlemen opposite. Let us give some hope to the man who is looking to the future; let us hold out some encouragement, some reward for individual endeavour, to the boy who is looking upward rather than down at the ground. Do not tell him in advance that because he knows how to handle an aeroplane he is not going to get a licence. Do not tell him in advance that while the minister can give him a licence, the board can cancel it. Do not tell him that you are not going to give him a licence for fear he may compete with someone else. After going through the conflict; after having grasped the opportunity to do his duty for his country; after having taken his chance and accepted the risk, he will come back here full of fire, of faith and of fight. He will realize that competition and healthy rivalry, yes, that the struggle involved in giving service to our people, are the very lifeblood of this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This is where I came in.
My hon. friend says that is the right thing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No; I said "This is where I came in."

Yes; well, I will say that is where my hon. friend will go out. The people of this country, neither' old nor young, will ever stand for that one big monopoly. If my hon. friend thinks some of our monopolies are too big now, what about the one big one ' he would bring about? Who is going to run

Aeronautics Act
it? It would seem that we are going to nationalize everything. Who will be the operator?
There will be no profit.
We shall not need elections.
And what about the sheriff?

Someone refers to the sheriff. Well, the sheriff may come in. He may come in before my hon. friends take over; and he will certainly come in in a national way after my friends have taken over.
I do not wish to speak at length, except to say that the principle of free enterprise, the old principle whereby a man hopes for a reasonable reward in return for his own efforts, is the thing that will bring this country back. We cannot pull ourselves up by our shoelaces. We cannot legislate ourselves out of competition. Why, you might as well legislate yourself out of circulation.
Hon. members in this chamber know about the development in the automobile industry. I do not expect that either they or I will see the time when the aeroplane will be as generally recognized as a way of travel as the automobile has been. But we do know that in the next few years many of our young men, who are now in the services, and who may have dreams, will try to fulfil those dreams. I have heard them say that they want to club together, to build up a few thousand dollars so that they can establish a company to give service into the north country.
As the hon. member for York South said this afternoon-
York West. You are getting all mixed up.

And you have been mixed up most of the time since you have been here, and you have not been here long.
I can well recall being at Red Lake in 1936, and I recall the pride of those aeroplane operators, who risked their lives every day. The hon. member for Fort William would know some of them well. We know that since that time some have lost their lives. They were the men who risked their lives in those little, old wobbly planes. True, they were not very safe to ride in, but some of us risked riding in them. They twisted and squirmed, but they got to Red Lake. And those boys, with a sense of pride, referred to their trips to Red Lake. It made their chests swell with pride when they said, "There is more freight comes in here every day by air than is coming into any airport in the United States of America."
That is what has happened in that north country. And then my hon. friends to my left
would say, "No; we will determine it by this parliament. We will get a group of politicians in the house to say whether or not we can go to certain points and find gold, or find ore that has mineral value in that great north country."
Again, as the hon. member for York West said, perhaps there were some who lost their money when they were taken in by air. But that was not the fault of the aeroplane; it was the fault of what they saw when they got there, or through their lack of good judgment.
But in the northern parts of Quebec, in the great Yellowknife district, and in the Northwest Territories-in all these areas where there are no railways, development would not have been as rapid, had it not been for the risks these men have taken, and the aeroplane service that has been provided.
Therefore I say I am opposed to the principle embodied in this bill, a bill bristling with domination by the minister, bristling with a continuation of regimentation which is so distasteful in a time of war, and certainly should never be perpetuated in peace time. I say this in all kindliness to the minister. Someone said to me that if there was to be a dictator it might as well be the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and I was inclined to agree with that, because, as I have said, he was a good engineer in some respects. And, if we have to be engineered, probably we might as well be engineered by the Minister of Munitions and Supply as by anyone else.
The people do not want this kind of bill. I do not believe they have ever voted for a bill of this kind. I do not believe they have ever been told before an election that we were going to put this great new enterprise into some new form of strait-jacket, and that we must leave to the minister the decision as to who shall or who shall not have air routes.
I must say, however, that I think the minister could and should amend this bill. He could amend it so that the board would function as does the board of transport commissioners. He could sit on a commission of that kind, and would not only add dignity, but give assistance. I think the minister should say that he will give a free chance to those who can give the assurance that they have the necessary funds and the necessary aircraft to carry passengers safely. If a group of young men ask for a permit, whether they favour the government or do not favour it; if they return from overseas and snow by their skill and ingenuity, and what they have behind them, that they want to establish a route into some district, and want to develop the country and take the risk, then I say that there should be some rule under which there
Aeronautics Act

would be equality of opportunity for those men, in this great and promising enterprise of the future. Probably we in parliament might not have as great an imagination as those young men will have.
I do not believe the enterprise should be strangled to the point where we can say who can or who cannot enter into this type of development. Surely we can regulate matters so that, once they get into the air, they will not run into each other. Surely, if we can regulate at all, we can do that. I agree that we should not grant licences to people to carry our men, women and children in aircraft which would not stand up to any reasonable mechanical tests.
We shall not be short of men to operate aircraft. There will be thousands of them, even after taking account of those grand pilots who have been lost. We shall have thousands of men after this war who will be dreaming of taking their places in work of this kind. They will read this bill and say, "What does this mean? Does it mean that we cannot organize a company? Does it mean that we cannot get a licence? Does it mean that licences can be cancelled, at will? Does it mean that the Trans-Canada Air Lines can get anything they like to complete their service and monopolize the business? Does it mean that the Canadian National Railways, because they are experienced in transportation, and because they know something about air travel, should be eliminated? Does it mean that Canadian Pacific Air Lines must be eliminated?"

What do you think it
means?

I should like to hear what the Minister of Agriculture thinks it means? I would say that it means as much to free enterprise in the future as the Saskatchewan elections meant to the future possibilities of your party.
And yours.
Ours will still be living after yours is gone.

I can say this, anyway, that we at least did not lose anything in Saskatchewan. However, it will be observed that ministers on the government benches are trying to divert the issue from the one before the Chair. I shall not detain the committee, but I say to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, in conclusion, that I have spoken in all sincerity, and I have meant just what I have said.
What have you said?

Well, the Minister of Agriculture cannot read the newspaper and listen

to me at the same time. I say in all sincerity that this does smack of socialism. I have no apology to make for free enterprise. I know something about what has made this country what it is. I know what a day's work is. I know what it is to start from scratch. I have seen some of our best men start from scratch, as one might term it. I can see all these delightful young men and women, the finest generation that has ever been bom in this dominion. Even though the best of them may be killed overseas, the rest will be better than we have ever been. I am thinking of their future, and I know they will want some room for their imagination, some room for their enterprise. They will not want to be strangled and strait-jacketed. They will not want it left to one man to define their course, to be master of their future interests instead of themselves.

I should like to ask the
minister one or two questions before the section carries. The first has to do with the position of United States air lines that may try to obtain permission to fly routes in Canada. As I read the bill, there is no restriction on any air line, whether it is Canadian or not, obtaining a licence, but.of course all other transportation companies are prohibited from getting a licence. I wish to know if there is anything to prevent a United States company from applying for a licence to fly between two points in Canada. Personally I think it would be a great mistake if it could be done, but there are rumours that some United States air companies would like to do that and are laying their plans accordingly. I suggest that the minister should clear up that situation.
The next question has to do with the route from Canada to Australia and New Zealand. The prime ministers of those countries were here within the last few weeks, and I have no doubt there have been some developments with regard to air routes across the Pacific. The minister should tell us what he can of those developments. My understanding is that most of the flying in Australia is done by a shipping company. I was told that a few weeks ago by a leading civil servant from Australia and I ask the minister to correct me if I am wrong. I questioned this official very closely on that point and I do not think there is any doubt about it. There may be Canadian shipping companies on either coast that could set up and operate air routes in connection with their steamship lines.
^ Representations have been made about this bill which I think should be brought to the attention of the minister and the committee. I have here a bulletin dated May 30, 1944,

Aeronautics Act
issued by the air industries and transport association of Canada. It deals with various questions having to do with aviation. As the minister knows, the association is made up of all the air companies in Canada, including Trans-Canada Air Lines. The president this year is Mr. Noorduyn. The air transport companies which are members of the association are Trans-Canada Air Lines, Canadian Pacific Air Lines, Laurentian Air Services Limited, M. and C. Aviation Company Limited and Northern Airways Limited. The associate members are British Overseas Airways Corporation and United Air Lines Transport Corporation. There are also listed as members about one hundred companies having to do with the air industry or air transportation. These include companies building aeroplanes, parts and so on. I have not counted them, but there must be at least one hundred. I should like to quote from page four of the bulletin as follows:
Indications are that this new central authority is to be built up around the existing civil aviation division of the Department of Transport of which division the Minister of Munitions and Supply is the head.
True, this action will centralize all regulatory powers relating to air transport but from information available this board will be only an advisory body with final authority vested in the minister.
Those seven last words are underlined.
It will certainly not be the "central, free and independent authority" which the directors had in mind when they framed their resolution at the last annual meeting.
Apparently at the last annual meeting of this association a resolution was passed requesting that there be set up a central, free and independent authority. The bulletin goes on:
There is no change in the situation whereby the officials most concerned with the granting of licences are the deputy minister of transport and the director of air services, while the superintendent of air and land mail services is doubtless vitally concerned with the granting of air mail contracts. These gentlemen are all directors of the government owned air line, consequently it is little wonder that operators view this divided responsibility as being incompatible with a sense of impartial and disinterested treatment, particularly should there be a clashing of government and private interests.
This "central, free and independent government authority for civil aviation" should be established on the lines of the board of transport commissioners, which is an independent regulatory body whose rulings are binding and conclusive. Appeals from the rulings of the authority can be only to the supreme court on points of law and on points of fact to the governor in council.
Such independence alone can engender in the minds of operators the feeling that applications for air transport licences, prompted by present and future public convenience and necessity, will be considered equitably and on their merits.
That is a representation which merits the most careful consideration by the minister.
Does my hon. friend believe it is good government to delegate governmental responsibility to independent boards?

I have taken the stand from the start that this board should be a judicial board of the same type as the board of transport commissioners. On that the minister and I appear to disagree. I think he is wrong and I have no doubt he thinks I am wrong. I propose to read also a copy of a telegram from the Vancouver board of trade to the Prime Minister, dated June 28, 1944. I think the Vancouver board of trade has over two thousand members. It is strictly non-political; members of all political parties belong to it. The president last year or the year before was one of the leading Liberals in British Columbia, a former member of the provincial house. The telegram reads:
Regarding bill one thirty three an act to amend the Aeronautics Act. We endorse principle of an air transport board but respectfully suggest section seven be amended to read five members instead of three for reason that Pacific coast should be recognized on board by one representative. Sections nine and ten and twelve should provide for appeal from board to governor in council instead^ of minister. Further we recommend that section twelve be amended by placing full responsibility in board for issue of licences. We further recommend that appeal in subsection ten of section twelve should be from board to governor general m council. Cannot stress too strongly principle that control of powers outlined in bill should be in hands governor general in council rather than minister.
On the coast we are particularly concerned about having an independant board to rule on these questions. I have also a copy of a letter, which I do not propose to read, from the Montreal board of trade to the Prime Minister.
It has been this way for fifty years. When the railroad propaganda machine rolls, every board of trade and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association snaps into line.

The minister is going too far in that statement. I do not know anything about the Montreal board of trade, but I do not think he is right about that body. This letter is signed by the President, Henry G. Birks, one of the most responsible and finest of Canadian citizens. I do not think either he or his council can be charged with *speaking for any interest. They wrote to the Prime Minister on July 4 setting out in great detail and, in my opinion, logically, suggestions with regard to this bill, and if the minister has not seen that letter I would suggest that he go over it very carefully.
