So far as the Vancouver board of trade is concerned, I strongly resent the statement of the minister. He said that all boards of trade-and that covers men in every city and town of Canada and some of the most responsible men in every city and town- always speak for the railways or for some interest, or words to that effect.
I did not say anything of the kind.

I think the minister for his own sake should make clear that he spoke out of turn when he said that, because he is absolutely wrong and it is maligning a group of men who are among the finest citizens of this country. They have done wonderful work on behalf of Canada and are doing it every day of the week.
So much for those representations. I have no doubt that there have been many other representations made by responsible bodies across Canada, and I suggest to the minister that this bill should be given further consideration. The minister and I both came into the house together, having been elected in 1935. As someone has said, the minister is a great engineer, and I think he has made a great success of many of the things that he has undertaken here, but I have noticed that several times this house has been asked to rush through some bill for the minister giving him the widest possible authority, giving him, in fact, a blank cheque, which is what this very bill does; then in a year or two the minister finds that it was a mistake, that everything is wrong and he comes back with another bill which we have to rush through for him. That is exactly what happened with the Transport Act; much the same thing happened with the provision for agreed charges; it was forced through the house. Such procedure is not good enough. Nobody is perfect, not even on this side of the house. The minister makes mistakes too, and in this bill I think he has made several mistakes. I suggest in all earnestness that he give the bill further consideration in view of the suggestions and representations which have been made respecting it. It might still be possible to introduce a bill this session which would meet with the approval of all sides of the house. I would ask the minister to answer the two questions I have asked.

I have explained to the
committee several times the procedure with regard to applications from citizens of other countries. If an air line in the United States wishes to operate between points in Canada or between a point in the United States and

some point in Canada, it must first go to the civil aeronautics board of its own country and file an application for the route with its own board.
Even if it were flying between two Canadian points?

Yes. We do not deal with the nationals of other countries. That is by international agreement. If any United States air line wishes to fly in Canada, it must first go to its own aeronautics board and obtain a certificate of necessity and approval of the route.
What right would any United States board have to issue approval of a route between two points in Canada?
Simply the right we have conferred upon them to designate'the nationals of their country who have sound reasons for flying over a route in Canada.
Who is "we"?
What kind of question is that?
You said "we" have conferred upon them. I am wondering who is "we".
The Canadian government, the people of Canada.
The people of Canada do not do it. It must be some governmental authority.	.

I have explained the procedure four or five times, but perhaps the hon. member does not follow the proceedings very closely. The international agreement to which I refer has been tabled, and my hon. friend could clear up the point by having the Clerk produce the agreement for him.
Does not that regulation apply only for a route from a United States point to a Canadian point?
No. I can assure my hon. friend that we do not accept applications from other nationals. That is covered by international agreement.
Is there anything to prevent a United States company from setting up a subsidiary in Canada which would apply for a licence and be permitted to operate in that way?

If they are permitted to incorporate a Canadian company, and the company has Canadian personnel and Canadian pilots, I presume they could do it. But the directors must be Canadian citizens, and seventy-five per cent of the stock must be owned in Canada.

What act is that provision in?
It is under the regulations of the Aeronautics Act.
Should that not be in this bill?

It is not desirable to print
all the regulations in the act. The provision is just as effective if it is in a regulation. Under the act regulations can be drawn, and regulations are sometimes amended by international agreement.

Should not the stock be
owned 100 per cent instead of only seventy-five per cent in Canada?

It happens to be seventy-five per cent. It is reciprocal. If my hon. friend is interested in the wording of the regulation, it reads as follows:
No aircraft shall be registered in Canada unless (a) it is a civil aircraft owned by a British subject or subjects or by a company or corporation created or incorporated under and subject to the laws of any part of His Majesty's dominions, of which the president and two-thirds or more of the directors and other managing officers thereof are British subjects and in which at least seventy-five per centum of the voting interest is owned or controlled by British subjects, or unless (b) it is a civil aircraft owned by His Majesty in the right of Canada or any of the provinces of Canada or of any other of His Majesty's dominions.

Is that point not very apt
to come up after the war when the Americans are trying to expand their flying?

The international agreement between Canada and the United States can be amended only by mutual consent, and it is not likely to be seriously amended. The approach from a United States corporation must be through the civil aeronautics board of the United States to the state department of the United States, then to the Department of External Affairs of Canada, and then the application would be in a position to be considered by the proper authorities in Canada, which in future will be the air transport board -if I ever succeed in passing this amendment.

Would the minister answer
my other question about Australia?

The airway service that
operates all externally, so far as I know, is the Quantus Airways which are owned jointly, I believe, by certain interests in Australia and by Overseas Airways. Quantus Airways is not, so far as I know, associated with any shipping company. In any event it is purely an air company, of which Overseas Airways,
which is the chosen instrument of the Briitsh government, owns forty-nine per cent of the stock.

There is no restriction in
Australia against any transportation company engaging in the aircraft business.

That may be so, but, so far as I know, no shipping company or railway company in Australia operates aircraft.
Some hon. member opposite mentioned the fact that there are internal air lines in Britain in which the railways have an interest. I think it is only an interest; whether a majority or minority interest I do not know. Furthermore, it is an association of railways rather than any one railway that has the investment. I am thinking of Scottish aviation. Civil aviation in England is not as extensive as it is in the maritime provinces; it is a very small operation. All aviation outside the British empire is operated by the chosen instrument of the government, which has no railway or shipping interest.

One more question with
regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company divesting themselves of any interest in air lines. Take an operation such as Consolidated Smelting. They would very likely want to establish an air line to service their outlying property, let us say, up in the Yellowknife district, to service their mine. Consolidated Smelting and Refining, I understand, is certainly affiliated with, if not controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Would they be allowed under the regulations to operate an airway or not, irrespective of the fact that they happened to be primarily a mining operation? I foresee in the future a great number of operators who will be primarily engaged in one line, but who will wish to operate an air line on the side for their own and possibly for the public service as well.

Any mining or other company can operate a service for the carrying of their own goods. There is no difficulty about that under the act, and there never has been; nor is there any difficulty under this bill. If, however, they wish to be common carriers and to accept carriage for hire they come under this bill. The question whether Consolidated Smelting and Refining is a railway operation could be looked into and a decision made when the question was raised. The provision is not a definite prohibition. It is a prohibition restricted in the public interest, and if it is in the public interest for Consolidated Smelters to operate an air line I have no doubt the permit will be issued.

There is nothing in the bill to make it impossible for the, board so to recommend or for the minister so to act.

I foresee the possibility of their operating a line for their own service and a community growing up, as there is now in the Yellowknife district, and the Consolidated company being asked to provide a service for the benefit of the remote community up there, so that they would become common carriers as well as a company carrier. That has happened in the past, and it is the sort of thing I foresee in the future.
If the transport board should recommend such an operation in the public interest, there is nothing in the bill to make it impossible.

Certainly.

In this part, unless the context otherwise requires, "minister" means the Minister of Transport or such other minister as the governor in council may from time to time designate, except that in any matter relating to defence, "minister" means the Minister of National Defence for Air.
The Minister of Transport is not even here to-day and has not had anything whatever to do with this bill since it has been before the house. Why is that?
Does my hon. friend want me to go over again the explanation I have made at least twelve times? If he is putting on a filibuster, let him say so.

As long as the governor in council so decides.

If that is the plan, why does it not so appear in the bill? Why does the bill not name the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and let the governor in council designate somebody else when the time comes? Why is the section worded in the way it is?

The minister must not think-

There is a question in my mind arising out of something that was implanted there when the Minister of National Defence for Air made a statement several months ago. We should consider the implications of this section before it carries. In effect this section sets up a board of three members with extensive powers, subject, of course, to the minister. This board will hold office during good behaviour for ten years, the first three members being appointed for periods of ten, nine and eight years. I think it is wise to give a considerable degree of permanency to the members of this board, but we are living in peculiar times. The boys who are and will be interested in civil aviation are now overseas. I should like to point out to the minister that this board should not be appointed for so long a time as this bill contemplates. We are going through a transition period. Our best skilled personnel, from the point of view of both transportation and management are now overseas. They are engaged in work that will qualify them better than any other individuals for this particular work. Events are taking place to-day which may change the whole aspect of civil transportation within the next few years. Because of that I think the minister should reconsider the length of time during which this first board will hold office. I realize that there may be difficulty in getting the right type

of men to act. I agree that they should be given time to grow into their jobs and that there should be considerable permanency in their appointments. But because of the abnormal conditions through which we are passing, and because air transportation is in its infancy and the men best skilled to do this work are serving overseas acquiring the knowledge that will fit them to do this work, we should leave the door open so that the personnel of this board may be composed of men who are otherwise engaged at the present time. I believe that we should not postpone it for ten, nine and eight years. Ten years is a long time in the life of an airman and the war veterans who will come back and who may have an opportunity to take these responsible jobs. We should keep every possible channel open for the men who have served in the air force during this war, men who have had experience in air transportation matters and in managerial positions. When they come back they should be given an opportunity of obtaining the very best jobs there are in civil transportation. I would urge the minister to cut down the period of ten, nine and eight years to at least five, four and three years in order to give those men that opportunity. I would go so far as to say three, two and one year, but that would be only a guess as to the length of the war. I am giving that as an illustration to .exhort the minister not to appoint this board for as long a time as this bill contemplates. Might I have an opinion on this matter?

Very careful consideration has been given to the problem. The term is the same as the term of the members of the board of transport commissioners. The purpose of the board is to build up a jurisprudence, and to obtain the assistance of experienced men in developing an air transport policy for Canada. It is the view of the government that this board should have permanency in order that it may be a permanent guide to an air transport policy for Canada. I can assure my hon. friend that men overseas with suitable experience will be fully considered, in fact are being fully considered for appointment to this board. The work requires a vast background of experience, and a highly developed technical training in order to give the type of service that we wish. These are not political jobs, not jobs to hand out because you like a person. They are jobs that require intensive training, and I can assure my hon. friend that in the making of the appointments the qualifications of those overseas will be very carefully examined.
fMr. Boucher.]

May I point out to the minister that I can see the reason for having the very best personnel possible free from political preference. I would not impugn a thing like that to a board of this kind. I trust it would not get down to that. The experience of the type of man we should like to have on this board has been expanding daily within the last month, and will go on during the war in the Pacific which may follow. If we appoint men with the experience of to-day, we shall be excluding men whose knowledge and experience are improving from day to day. If we appoint this board for ten, nine and eight years, it will exclude those young men who are to-day gaining experience from holding these jobs during the efficient period of their young lives. Our personnel may entirely change within the next two, three or four years, and we may find ourselves in a position where we are at least duty bound or morally bound, having appointed men to the board for ten, nine and eight years, to keep them there, although we may have others more fit and worthy and more capable of holding the appointments. We shall not be able to hold out to our boys who are acquiring experience to-day over the battlefields any hope of reaching this office. I think it is a mistake to make these appointments for such long periods of time at the very beginning. I appreciate the fact that once the board is established, once we change over to civil aviation instead of military aviation, the situation will be different, and then perhaps ten years will not be too long a term. I think, however, we should leave the door open for new appointments, after the board is first set up.

I have not
taken any part at all in this discussion, although there are many features I should like to have cleared up. I agree with the hon. member for Carleton that the initial appointments are for too long. It seems to me that eight, nine and ten years is too long to appoint these men, from the very first. I believe that it is always a good thing for a body of this kind to have new blood from time to time, or at least that those appointed in the first instance, having proved their worth and shown that they possessed the confidence of the country, might be reappointed. I feel very strongly that the members of this board should not be appointed for these long periods. I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken, that the initial appointments should be for three, four and five years, or even three, seven and ten years, so that new appointments or reappointments may be made in due course. I believe that would strengthen

An integral part of such a position would be that he shall not sell or hire or take advantage of his position. What has been said has not been directed toward his qualifications.
I think the hon. member has struck the nail on the head. The section beats around the
bush. The very substance of the matter is to prevent a person from using his previous employment for personal advantage, to the detriment of the board of which he may be a member. This section should be worded to cover a condition of that kind. I think there is a very strong reason why the motive of the section should be made more clear. There should be a prohibition against the commercial use of a man's earlier obligations and entanglements. The minister would be wise to take this matter into consideration and have the section amended in a proper way, instead of circling around it.

As I see it, we might use the words, "No member of the board shall sell any goods, or hire out any property, or render any service to the board for reward; and no member of the board shall be a shareholder, member, director or partner of any company, association or firm selling any goods or hiring out any property or giving any service to the board for reward."

The board is not in business; it buys nothing and sells nothing. It is advisory to the minister. It seems perfectly nonsensical that such a provision should be inserted, when the only thing a member could sell would probably be pencils and stationery- and even those come from the king's printer. We should not be absurd about this.
What salaries are to be paid to members of the board?
The measure says they will be fixed by order in council.
Can the minister give any idea of the salaries?
That has not been considered.

The minister has not
answered my question with regard to an air route from Canada to Australia and New Zealand. Can he give us any further information on that?
It is being considered.
There is no further announcement to be made.

No.

On section 6-part II-new section 9-Investigation and surveys.

I should imagine that in connection with investigation and surveys assistance by way of technical help and
Aeronautics Act

engineers would be required. Can the minister say what plans he has in mind in that connection?

The air services branch of the Department of Transport has highly trained technicians who could assist the board, and doubtless the board will be able to obtain any technical assistance it needs from within the department.
Is the board not to have technical assistance of its own?
If necessary, but it is not believed it will be necessary. The board is more a planning board. If technical work is to be done, the resources of the department will be at hand.
It is not intended to have experts working directly under the board?
It is possible, but not probable.

On section 6-part II-new section 11- Regulations.

I am suggesting that this section be amended by inserting the following as paragraph (i) after paragraph (h):
Prescribe maximum hours and other working conditions for pilots and co-pilots employed by any air carrier.
The remaining paragraphs will be relettered (j), (k) and (1).

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I move accordingly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The amendment seems to be one that will be particularly welcome. There does not seem to be much chance of this bill being completed to-night, and I wonder if the minister would allow this to stand as a notice so that it may be dealt with the next time the bill is in committee.

I was hopeful that the bill would pass, because unfortunately I must be away on business next week. It is a simple amendment I am proposing, which permits the board to make specific regulations to deal with working hours for pilots and co-pilots.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am with the minister in his desire to get this bill through, but there might be employees other than pilots and co-pilots to be considered. What about groundcrews and other employees?
Those are subject to the Department of Labour. Piloting is more a profession than a craft, although there is a pilots' association.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is a question of safety.
There are security matters to be considered. The other employees of an air company would ordinarily have a union agreement. In fact such employees have union agreements with the management already.

This section brings up many different points. Even if it were carried before eleven o'clock there is no possible chance that section 12 would be carried to-night. I suggest that the section be left over in order that we may consider this change in section 11.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
While this amendment
is being considered, I should like to call the minister's attention to another matter. This section sets out the specific types of regulations which the board may make. In looking through the Railway Act, T find that sections 316 to 347 set out the specific powers of the board of transport commissioners to prohibit discriminatory practices so far as rates and other matters are concerned. The sections in the Railway Act are quite specific. A company cannot give undue preference or discriminate against customers, nor can it do anything that is prejudicial. There is a great list of things that the railway companies must not do in the way of discriminatory practices. The question of the control of free transportation is referred to in the act. In fact, it is here that I find that members of parliament are accorded passes on the railways. I am not stressing the point, but it may be that some of us may hope to get the odd trip on the T.C.A. I am asking the minister if it would not be desirable to grant some power to this board so that it may prevent discriminatory or unfair practices on the part of the air lines.

It is the intention that a provision of that type will be included in the regulations. The purpose of the amendment to the act is to permit the aeronautics board to build up its own jurisprudence, just as the board of transport commissioners has built up jurisprudence over the years. In 1938 we attempted to apply the regulations that had been built up for the railroads to transport by air, and we arrived at some absurd situations. I could mention several that were quite proper under railroad operation, but which did not apply to air. Purposely we have not attempted to tie the hands of the board, but rather we have intended to give the board the power to make provisions applicable to the air.

Questions

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I think I sense what the minister is saying, but I would call his attention to the fact that the Railway Act contains specific provisions.
We could write in the regulation about passes, but that does not apply to transport by air. You simply cannot carry free passengers by air.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Could you not have a short clause which would give the board power to make regulations of that kind, or is there a clause hidden in the bill which I have not seen?

My hon. friend will notice that paragraph (k) provides that the board may make regulations providing for the effective carrying out of the provisions of this part. That is an omnibus clause that allows the board to pass anything it likes.
